docs.title: English Pronunciation (SSBE)
docs.text: Personal project: a structured method to teach and improve English pronunciation, aimed at native Spanish speakers. Reference accent is SSBE (Southern Standard British English, also called RP / BBC / Queen's English), with the main differences to General American noted throughout.

docs.title: Origin story
docs.text:
I started years ago to improve my English, especially my speaking. I realised the first thing I had to do was learn pronunciation.

Everyone talks about comprehensible input, how children learn, and it makes sense. But my own experience, and what I saw in others, is that no matter how many series and films you watch, the improvement is slight, especially in speaking and listening. There are things we do not understand when natives speak. It is not magic. So I decided to learn pronunciation properly.

Where do you start? With the vowels; they are the most important phonemes in any language. I had heard English has twelve to fourteen vowels; it sounded crazy. I watched general articulation videos on YouTube, then went vowel by vowel through all twelve. A big jump. Then the consonants: English has around ten or eleven that do not exist in Spanish. That opened up a world that blew my mind.

With the phonemes in place I focused on words, and understood how important the schwa is: the weakening of unstressed syllables, a phenomenon that does not exist in Spanish. Then, just when I thought I had words under control, I discovered connected speech, linking, assimilation, elision, which changes everything. The same weakening inside a word happens across whole phrases: function words reduce, content words carry the stress.

IPA decision: I considered learning the IPA formally but chose not to; it seemed too complex. Yet as I studied each phoneme I learned the IPA implicitly. It is now my best tool: I look up a word's transcription in a dictionary and I know how it is pronounced without hearing it.

English is not phonetic; it is not written as it is spoken. So the real question is: given a written word, how do you know how to say it? There are rules, around eight written ones and many unwritten ones. They fail sometimes but hold in a great many cases. This project collects them in one place.

docs.title: Why this exists
docs.text:
Comprehensible input alone (watching series, films) improved speaking and listening only slightly. The jump came from studying pronunciation explicitly, bottom-up: phonemes first, then words, then connected speech, then rhythm and intonation.

Inventory learned: 24 consonants, 12 vowels, 8 diphthongs, 5 triphthongs. 49 phonemes total, many more than Spanish.

IPA decision: did not study IPA formally. Learning each phoneme implicitly taught it. IPA is now the primary tool: look up the dictionary transcription and the pronunciation is known without hearing the word.

docs.title: The learning path
docs.text:
1. Vowels. The most important phonemes in any language.
  2. Consonants. Focus on the 10-11 that do not exist in Spanish.
  3. Syllables and words. Stress and the schwa in unstressed syllables.
  4. Connected speech. Linking, assimilation, elision.
  5. Sentence level. Weak forms, content vs function words.
  6. Rhythm and intonation. English is stress-timed; Spanish is syllable-timed.

docs.title: Core principle
docs.text: The biggest error for Spanish speakers is forcing a full vowel into every syllable, as written, instead of using the schwa. Even schwa deletion is something Spanish speakers never do. Prioritize the schwa above everything.

docs.title: Connected speech and phonology
docs.text: What happens to a vowel inside a word (unstressed → schwa) also happens at the sentence level: whole function words weaken, and content words carry the stress. English is stress-timed; Spanish is syllable-timed. This changes everything about rhythm and intelligibility.

docs.title: Linking
docs.text: Semivowels inserted between words to link them: yod /j/, R, and W. Plus the general linking of final consonant to following vowel.

docs.title: Assimilation
docs.text: Adjacent sounds influence each other (e.g. /dj/ → /dʒ/ in "during").

docs.title: Elision
docs.text: Sounds dropped in connected speech.

docs.title: Geminates / twinning
docs.text: Two identical adjacent sounds merge.

docs.title: T and D phenomena
docs.text:
• Drop T: common in connected speech.
  • Glottal T stop: replaces T in many positions; heavy in some British accents. Obama's "certain" is a cited example.
  • Drop D: e.g. "and" → /ən/; friend/friends in fast speech.
  • Stop plosives / unreleased plosives.
  • American T: flap t in unstressed syllables.

docs.title: Drop H
docs.text: Function words with H lose it in connected speech (him, her, have).

docs.title: Weak forms
docs.text: Function words have a weak (schwa) form in connected speech: - was, been, from, of/off, and, can/can't. Content words keep strong forms; function words reduce. Reductions and contractions are very important.

docs.title: Rhythm and intonation
docs.text:
• Stress-timed rhythm: stressed syllables fall at regular intervals; unstressed syllables compress.
  • Intonation changes meaning; thought groups chunk the utterance.
  • Uptalk is a notable intonation pattern.

docs.title: Consonant clusters
docs.text: More common in English than Spanish. Two typical Spanish errors: 1. Inserting an E before initial S-clusters (school, Spain). 2. Mispronouncing final consonants and final clusters (rare in Spanish).

docs.title: Consonant: /tʃ/ (CH)
docs.text: Producible for most Spanish speakers (it exists in Spanish "ch"), but the spellings that hide it, and the contrast with /ʃ/, need attention.

docs.title: 1. What it is
docs.text:
/tʃ/ is a voiceless postalveolar affricate: a /t/ immediately followed by /ʃ/, as in "church", "watch", "nature".

Spanish contrast: Spanish has /tʃ/ (the "ch" in "chico"), so production is easy. The issues are: which English spellings give /tʃ/ (not only "ch"), and not confusing it with /ʃ/.

docs.title: 2. How to produce it
docs.text: Stop the air with the tongue as for /t/ just behind the ridge, then release into /ʃ/. One quick sound, not two.

docs.title: 3. Angle 1 — spellings that make /tʃ/
docs.text: Spelling Examples ch church, cheese, much, teach, chair tch watch, match, kitchen, catch t (in -ture, -tu-) nature, future, culture, question, actual ti (some) (compare /ʃ/ in -tion)

docs.title: 4. Angle 2 — where the /tʃ/ sound is written
docs.text: ch: church, cheese, much, teach, chair, child, rich, each. tch: watch, match, kitchen, catch, fetch, switch. t + ure/u: nature, future, culture, adventure, picture, question, actual, virtual, situation (yod -> /tʃ/ by assimilation).

docs.title: 5. Minimal pairs / contrasts
docs.text: Pair Contrast chair / share /tʃ/ vs /ʃ/ cheap / sheep /tʃ/ vs /ʃ/ (and vowel) chop / shop /tʃ/ vs /ʃ/ catch / cash /tʃ/ vs /ʃ/ choose / shoes /tʃ/ vs /ʃ/

docs.title: 6. Common Spanish error
docs.text: The trap: not knowing -ture and -tu- give /tʃ/ (nature, culture, actual), and softening /tʃ/ into /ʃ/. The fix: keep the /t/ stop at the start of the sound. Learn the -ture pattern. Contrast chair/share.

docs.title: 7. Practice
docs.text: See study links: assimilation and /j/-drop resources (nature, culture come from t + yod).

docs.title: Consonant: dark L /ɫ/
docs.text: English has two L sounds. The "dark" L, at the end of syllables, does not exist in Spanish and distorts the vowels around it.

docs.title: 1. What it is
docs.text:
English L has two variants: - Light (clear) L: before a vowel, as in "light", "love". Close to Spanish L. - Dark L /ɫ/: after a vowel or at syllable end, as in "table", "full", "milk".

Spanish contrast: Spanish has only the light L. Spanish speakers use a light L everywhere, so "milk" and "table" sound wrong. The dark L also colours the preceding vowel.

docs.title: 2. How to produce it
docs.text: Dark L: keep the tongue tip down or lightly touching, and pull the BACK of the tongue up and back toward the soft palate. It sounds almost like a "w" or "o" colouring. In extreme cases it vocalises fully (L-vocalization): "milk" -> "miuk".

docs.title: 3. Angle 1 — when L is dark
docs.text: Position L type Examples before a vowel light light, love, lady, believe after a vowel / syllable-final dark full, milk, table, cold, help before a consonant dark milk, help, salt, old syllabic (C + le) dark table, castle, purple, little

docs.title: 4. Angle 2 — where dark L appears (word lists)
docs.text: table, travel, trouble, pencil, level, equal, model, nasal, annual, moral, royal, label, cancel, unveil, capitol, methanol, alcohol, control, lawful, full, milk, cold, help, salt, old, bottle, little, apple, people.

docs.title: 5. Minimal pairs / contrasts
docs.text: Pair Contrast light / right /l/ vs /r/ full (dark l) vs foo presence of dark l feel / fear dark l vs /ə/ (British) milk (dark) vs mick dark l colouring

docs.title: 6. Common Spanish error
docs.text: The trap: using a light Spanish L at the end of words (table, full, milk). The fix: pull the back of the tongue up and back for syllable-final L. Let it colour the vowel. Practise "level up" and words ending in -le.

docs.text: See study links: the Dark l resources (FluentU, Wikipedia L-vocalization, StackExchange) and "level up" on Youglish.

docs.title: Consonant: /h/
docs.text: A simple breath sound, but Spanish speakers either drop it or replace it with the harsh Spanish "j".

docs.title: 1. What it is
docs.text:
/h/ is a voiceless glottal fricative, just a push of breath, as in "house", "behind", "ahead".

Spanish contrast: the Spanish letter h is silent, and the Spanish "j" (jamón) is a harsh velar sound. Spanish speakers either drop the English /h/ entirely or replace it with that harsh /x/.

docs.title: 2. How to produce it
docs.text: Simply breathe out audibly before the vowel, with the mouth already in position for that vowel. No friction at the back of the throat, no Spanish "j". It is light.

docs.title: 3. Angle 1 — when a spelling makes /h/
docs.text: Spelling Pronounced? Examples h before a vowel yes house, happy, behind, ahead, hello h in wh- (some) yes (/h/) who, whole, whose silent h no hour, honest, heir, vehicle function words (weak) often dropped him, her, have (in connected speech)

docs.title: 4. Angle 2 — where the /h/ sound is written
docs.text: h: house, happy, behind, ahead, hello, help, hand, home, perhaps, ahead. wh (some): who, whole, whose, whom.

docs.title: h is pronounced by default; silent only in a short list
docs.text:
The useful framing: a written h before a vowel is pronounced, EXCEPT in these common silent-h words (learn them as a set):

  • hour, honest, honour, heir (and derivatives: honestly, heirloom).
  • vehicle, vehement, annihilate.
  • ghost, ghastly (gh), rhythm, rhyme (rh).
  • -ham place names: Durham, Nottingham, Birmingham, Chatham.
  • French loans: herb (US silent; UK pronounced), homage (varies).

Everywhere else, pronounce the h: history, hospital, hotel, horrible, human. See silent letters for the full silent-letter patterns.

docs.title: 5. Minimal pairs / contrasts
docs.text: Pair Contrast hair / air /h/ vs no onset heat / eat /h/ vs no onset hill / ill /h/ vs no onset hold / old /h/ vs no onset harm / arm /h/ vs no onset

docs.title: 6. Common Spanish error
docs.text: The trap 1: dropping /h/ so "house" = "ouse". The trap 2: using the harsh Spanish "j" (/x/) so "hello" sounds throaty. The fix: a light breath only. Contrast hair/air and heat/eat; the only difference is a soft puff of air.

docs.title: 7. Practice
docs.text: See study links: the drop-h resources (note: dropping is a native connected-speech feature for function words, different from the Spanish error of dropping content-word /h/).

docs.title: Consonant: /ŋ/ (NG)
docs.text: The sound at the end of "sing". It exists in Spanish only before other consonants, not as a word-final sound, and never with a following hard g.

docs.title: 1. What it is
docs.text:
/ŋ/ is a voiced velar nasal, the "ng" in "sing", "long", "thing".

Spanish contrast: Spanish has /ŋ/ only as an allophone before /k/ or /g/ (blanco, tango). It never ends a word in Spanish. Spanish speakers tend to add a hard /g/ (sing = "sing-g") or replace it with /n/.

docs.title: 2. How to produce it
docs.text: Raise the back of the tongue to the soft palate (as for /k/ or /g/) but send the air through the nose. Crucially, do NOT release a /g/ afterwards (in most positions).

docs.title: 3. Angle 1 — when a spelling makes /ŋ/
docs.text: Spelling Sound Examples ng (word-final) /ŋ/ (no g) sing, long, thing, song, ring ng + suffix /ŋ/ (no g) singer, singing, hanger ng (medial, some) /ŋg/ (with g) finger, longer, anger, hungry n before k/g /ŋ/ think, bank, uncle, drink

docs.title: 4. Angle 2 — where the /ŋ/ sound is written
docs.text: ng (final, no g): sing, long, thing, song, ring, king, bring, young, among, morning, nothing, evening. -inger/-inging: singer, singing, bringing, hanging. With a hard g (/ŋg/): finger, longer, anger, hungry, England, single, stronger. n before k: think, bank, drink, uncle, monkey, thank, link.

docs.title: 5. Minimal pairs / contrasts
docs.text: Pair Contrast sing / sin /ŋ/ vs /n/ thing / thin /ŋ/ vs /n/ ran / rang /n/ vs /ŋ/ sinner / singer /n/ vs /ŋ/ wing / win /ŋ/ vs /n/

docs.title: 6. Common Spanish error
docs.text: The trap 1: adding a hard g, so "sing" = "sing-g". The trap 2: replacing with /n/, so "sing" = "sin". The fix: back of tongue up, air through the nose, no g release at the end. Compare the native rule: finger has /ŋg/, but singer has only /ŋ/.

docs.title: Consonant: /r/
docs.text: The English R is nothing like the Spanish R. Getting it wrong marks a Spanish accent immediately.

docs.title: 1. What it is
docs.text:
/r/ is an approximant: the tongue approaches the roof of the mouth but never touches or vibrates. The sound in "red", "around", "very".

Spanish contrast: Spanish R is a tap or trill (the tongue taps or vibrates against the ridge). English R has no contact and no vibration. This is the single most accent-defining consonant.

Accent note: SSBE is non-rhotic, R is only pronounced before a vowel (red, very), not before a consonant or at the end (car, hard, mother have no R sound). American is rhotic and pronounces all of them.

docs.title: 2. How to produce it
docs.text: Curl or bunch the tongue back slightly so the tip points up toward the ridge but does NOT touch it. Round the lips a little. No tap, no trill. The tongue is still.

docs.title: 3. Angle 1 — when a spelling makes /r/ (British)
docs.text: Spelling Pronounced? Examples r before a vowel yes red, around, very, bright, carry r before consonant no (British) car(d), hard, park, first r word-final no (British) car, mother, far (unless linking to next vowel) rr yes (one /r/) carry, marry, mirror

docs.title: 4. Angle 2 — where the /r/ sound is written
docs.text:
Always the letter r or rr: red, run, around, very, bright, carry, marry, mirror, rural, iron, serenity, natural.

Linking R (British): a final written R is pronounced when the next word starts with a vowel: "far away", "mother and father".

docs.title: 5. Minimal pairs / contrasts
docs.text: Pair Contrast right / light /r/ vs /l/ road / load /r/ vs /l/ train / twain cluster clarity correct (tap vs approximant) Spanish tap vs English /r/

docs.title: 6. Common Spanish error
docs.text: The trap: tapping or trilling the R as in Spanish (perro/pero). The fix: no contact, no vibration. Tongue pulled back, lips slightly rounded. In British English, do not pronounce R before consonants or at the end of words.

docs.text: See study links: the R videos and tren/train contrast.

docs.title: Consonant: /ʃ/ (SH)
docs.text: Spanish speakers can produce it, but the problem is knowing which spellings hide it, far more than just written "sh".

docs.title: 1. What it is
docs.text:
/ʃ/ is a voiceless postalveolar fricative, the "sh" sound in "she", "mission", "sure".

Spanish contrast: standard Spanish has no /ʃ/, though some regions do (Río de la Plata, parts of Spain). The production is easy for most; the real problem is recognising the many spellings that produce it.

docs.title: 2. How to produce it
docs.text: Tongue bunched just behind the alveolar ridge, lips slightly rounded and pushed forward, push voiceless air. Like "s" but with the tongue pulled back and lips rounded.

docs.title: 3. Angle 1 — spellings that make /ʃ/
docs.text: Spelling Examples sh she, ship, shoe, cash, finish ti (in -tion) nation, station, question, patient ss (in -ssion) mission, discussion, pressure ci (in -cious/-cial) special, delicious, social, ancient si (in -sion after cons.) tension, mansion ch (French loans) machine, cache, chef, champagne s (before u) sure, sugar, assure

docs.title: 4. Angle 2 — where the /ʃ/ sound is written (word lists)
docs.text: session, mission, machine, cache, she, musician, politician, pressure, assure, impression, discussion, expression, permission, progression, transmission, possession, transition, visualization, special, social, delicious, nation, station, sure, sugar, chef.

docs.title: 5. Minimal pairs / contrasts
docs.text: Pair Contrast she / see /ʃ/ vs /s/ ship / sip /ʃ/ vs /s/ sheet / seat /ʃ/ vs /s/ shave / save /ʃ/ vs /s/ sham / Sam /ʃ/ vs /s/

docs.title: 6. Common Spanish error
docs.text: The trap: not realising a word has /ʃ/ (nation, sure, special) and saying /s/ or /tʃ/ instead. The fix: learn the spelling triggers (-tion, -ssion, -cious, -cial, s+u, French ch). The sound itself is easy; recognition is the work.

docs.title: Consonant: /ð/ (voiced TH)
docs.text: The voiced "th" in "this". Spanish has the sound only as an allophone, so speakers often replace it with /d/.

docs.title: 1. What it is
docs.text:
/ð/ is a voiced dental fricative, the "th" in "this", "mother", "breathe".

Spanish contrast: Spanish has a similar sound as the soft "d" between vowels (nada, cada), but not as a distinct phoneme at the start of words. Spanish speakers replace initial /ð/ with a hard /d/, so "this" becomes "dis".

docs.title: 2. How to produce it
docs.text: Tongue tip lightly between or against the top teeth, push voiced air with friction. It is the voiced partner of /θ/. The tongue touches the teeth, unlike /d/ (ridge) or /z/ (ridge).

docs.title: 3. Angle 1 — spellings that make /ð/
docs.text:
Always written th. /ð/ (voiced) appears in:

Position Examples function words (initial) the, this, that, these, those, they, them, then, there between vowels mother, father, brother, other, weather, together -the endings breathe, bathe, clothe, smooth

docs.title: 4. Angle 2 — where the /ð/ sound is written
docs.text: the, this, that, these, those, they, them, then, there, than, though, thus, mother, father, brother, other, another, weather, rather, together, either, breathe, bathe, clothe, smooth, with (often).

docs.title: 5. Minimal pairs / contrasts
docs.text:
Pair Contrast they / day /ð/ vs /d/ then / den /ð/ vs /d/ there / dare /ð/ vs /d/ breathe / breed /ð/ vs /d/ though / dough /ð/ vs /d/

Also /ð/ vs /z/: with/wizz, breathe/breeze.

docs.title: 6. Common Spanish error
docs.text: The trap: replacing /ð/ with a hard /d/, so "this" = "dis", "they" = "day". The fix: tongue to the teeth, voiced friction. Use the Spanish soft-d sound in "nada" as a starting point, then bring it to the front teeth.

docs.title: Consonant: /θ/ (voiceless TH)
docs.text: The voiceless "th" in "think". In most of Spain it matches the "z/c" sound (zapato), but Latin American speakers replace it with /s/ or /t/.

docs.title: 1. What it is
docs.text:
/θ/ is a voiceless dental fricative, the "th" in "think", "bath", "month".

Spanish contrast: European Spanish has this sound (the "z" and soft "c" in "zapato", "cielo"), so peninsular speakers produce it easily. Latin American Spanish uses /s/ (seseo), so those speakers replace /θ/ with /s/ or /t/.

docs.title: 2. How to produce it
docs.text: Tongue tip lightly between or against the top teeth, push voiceless air with friction. No voice. It is the voiceless partner of /ð/.

docs.title: 3. Angle 1 — spellings that make /θ/
docs.text:
Always written th. /θ/ (voiceless) appears in:

Position Examples content words (initial) think, thing, three, thunder, Thursday, theatre medial / final bath, month, both, tooth, north, healthy, author -th endings mouth (noun), path, cloth, breath, fourth

Contrast with /ð/: roughly, function words and -the verbs are voiced /ð/; content words and most -th endings are voiceless /θ/.

docs.title: 4. Angle 2 — where the /θ/ sound is written
docs.text: think, thing, three, thunder, thursday, theatre, theory, thick, thin, thread, bath, month, both, tooth, north, south, healthy, author, nothing, something, path, cloth, breath, fourth, mouth (noun), math, truth, death.

docs.title: 5. Minimal pairs / contrasts
docs.text: Pair Contrast think / sink /θ/ vs /s/ thing / sing /θ/ vs /s/ thin / tin /θ/ vs /t/ three / tree /θ/ vs /t/ bath / bat /θ/ vs /t/ mouth / mouse /θ/ vs /s/

docs.title: 6. Common Spanish error
docs.text: The trap: Latin American speakers use /s/ (think = sink) or /t/ (three = tree). The fix: tongue to the teeth, voiceless friction. Peninsular speakers can reuse their "z/c" sound directly.

docs.title: /θ/ - /ð/ alternation (noun vs verb)
docs.text:
Spelling marks it: nouns end -th (voiceless /θ/), verbs end -the (voiced /ð/): bath/bathe, breath/breathe, sheath/sheathe, teeth/teethe, wreath/wreathe. Also north/northern, south/southern, worth/worthy. See phoneme-spelling reference.

Position rules (from the source): - Initial th: /ð/ in function words (the, this, then, there); /θ/ in content words (think, through, throw). Exception: through /θ/. - Medial th + -er/-ing: usually /ð/ (other, brother, bathing). Exceptions: panther, ether, anything/nothing. - Final th: usually /θ/. Exceptions: with, smooth /ð/; booth, bequeath either.

docs.title: Consonant: /v/
docs.text: Does not exist in Spanish. Spanish b and v are the same sound, so speakers collapse /b/ and /v/.

docs.title: 1. What it is
docs.text:
/v/ is a voiced labiodental fricative: top teeth on the bottom lip, with voice and friction. The sound in "very", "love", "van".

Spanish contrast: in Spanish, b and v are pronounced identically (both a bilabial /b/ or /β/). Spanish speakers say /b/ where English needs /v/, so "very" becomes "berry".

docs.title: 2. How to produce it
docs.text: Rest the upper teeth lightly on the lower lip, push voiced air through so it buzzes. The lips do NOT come together (that would make /b/). It is the voiced partner of /f/.

docs.title: 3. Angle 1 — when a spelling makes /v/
docs.text: Spelling Examples v very, love, van, have, give, voice, service f (in "of") of (/ɒv/) ph (rare) Stephen

docs.title: 4. Angle 2 — where the /v/ sound is written
docs.text: Almost always v: very, love, van, have, give, voice, service, over, never, value, available, develop, visible, vowel, invest. Exception: "of" is /ɒv/. "Stephen" has /v/ for ph.

docs.title: 5. Minimal pairs / contrasts
docs.text:
The /b/ vs /v/ contrast is the core problem.

/v/ /b/ very berry van ban vest best vote boat vowel bowel curve curb

Also /v/ vs /f/ (voicing): van/fan, vine/fine, save/safe.

docs.title: 6. Common Spanish error
docs.text: The trap: pronouncing v as a Spanish b, so very = berry, vote = boat. The fix: teeth on lip, buzz. Keep the lips apart. Train /v/-/b/ pairs (very/berry, van/ban) until they are reliably different.

docs.title: Consonant: /w/
docs.text: A rounded glide. Spanish has a similar sound, but the b/v/w confusion and the hard-g insertion (huevo -> "güevo") carry over as errors.

docs.title: 1. What it is
docs.text:
/w/ is a voiced labial-velar approximant (glide), the sound in "water", "we", "quick".

Spanish contrast: Spanish has a /w/-like glide (hueso, cuando), so production is possible. Errors: inserting a hard /g/ before it (like "güevo"), or mixing it up with /b/ and /v/ (we/be/vee).

docs.title: 2. How to produce it
docs.text: Round the lips tightly and raise the back of the tongue, then glide quickly into the following vowel. No hard /g/ onset. Lips do not touch the teeth (that would be /v/) and do not close (that would be /b/).

docs.title: 3. Angle 1 — when a spelling makes /w/
docs.text: Spelling Examples w water, we, win, away, wonder, forward wh what, when, where, which, why (/w/ in most SSBE) u (after q, g) quick, queen, language, penguin, persuade o (in "one/once") one, once (/wʌn/)

docs.title: 4. Angle 2 — where the /w/ sound is written
docs.text: w: water, we, win, away, wonder, forward, well, work, want, world. wh: what, when, where, which, why, while, white, wheel. qu (= /kw/): quick, queen, question, quality, quiet, require. gu (= /gw/): language, penguin, anguish. u: persuade, suave. o: one, once.

docs.title: 5. Minimal pairs / contrasts
docs.text: Pair Contrast west / vest /w/ vs /v/ wine / vine /w/ vs /v/ we / be /w/ vs /b/ wet / vet /w/ vs /v/ worse / verse /w/ vs /v/

docs.title: 6. Common Spanish error
docs.text: The trap 1: inserting a hard g, so "water" gets a "gu" onset. The trap 2: confusing /w/, /v/, /b/ (west/vest, we/be). The fix: round the lips and glide, no g, no teeth, no lip closure. Contrast west/vest and we/be.

docs.text: See study links: consonant and minimal-pair resources.

docs.title: Consonant: /z/
docs.text: Does not exist in Spanish. Spanish s is always voiceless, so speakers miss the many English /z/ sounds, including most plural and verb endings.

docs.title: 1. What it is
docs.text:
/z/ is a voiced alveolar fricative: like /s/ but with voice (vocal cords buzzing). The sound in "zoo", "is", "please".

Spanish contrast: Spanish has no /z/; the letter s is always /s/. Spanish speakers devoice /z/ to /s/, so "is" becomes "iss" and "zoo" becomes "soo".

docs.title: 2. How to produce it
docs.text: Same tongue position as /s/ (tip near the alveolar ridge) but turn on the voice so it buzzes. It is the voiced partner of /s/.

docs.title: 3. Angle 1 — when a spelling makes /z/
docs.text:
Two spellings dominate: the letter z, and (very commonly) a single s between vowels. The letter z is almost always /z/.

Spelling Examples z (almost always /z/) zoo, zero, zebra, size, prize, lazy, dozen s between vowels easy, music, present, reason, visit, busy, cousin s in "is/was/as/his" is, was, as, his, has final s after voiced sound dogs, plays, loves (plural/3rd-person /z/) x (= /gz/) exam, exact, example, exist (see letter X rule) -se endings please, these, choose, cause, pause

Note on the letter z: it is /z/ in nearly every word. The rare exception is /ʒ/ in azure and seizure, and even those are often said with /z/. Compare also the single s between vowels, which is the other big /z/ source.

Note on ss: a doubled ss is NOT /z/; it is voiceless /s/ (pass, miss) or /ʃ/ (mission). Only five ss words take /z/: dessert, scissors, possess, dissolve, hussar. See double consonants.

docs.title: 4. Angle 2 — where the /z/ sound is written
docs.text: use, please, expose, tuesday, wednesday, thursday, close, was, lose, exam, exactly, exist, exemption, example, easy, is, as, realise, emphasize, size, advise, musician, cause, mouse, pause, amuse, because, excuse, refuse, monetization, rationalization, specialization, automatization.

docs.title: 5. Minimal pairs / contrasts
docs.text: /s/ /z/ ice eyes price prize bus buzz face phase loose lose racer razor

docs.title: 6. Common Spanish error
docs.text: The trap: devoicing every /z/ to /s/ (is = iss, zoo = soo), and getting plural/verb endings wrong. The fix: add voice. Same mouth as /s/, vocal cords on. Train /s/-/z/ pairs (ice/eyes, price/prize) and the plural rule (dogs = /z/, cats = /s/).

docs.title: 7. Practice
docs.text: See study links: the /z/ video and s/z endings resource.

docs.title: /s/ - /z/ alternation (noun vs verb)
docs.text:
Final -se varies between /s/ and /z/; some pairs are spelled to mark it: advice/advise, device/devise, and the UK pairs licence/license, practice/practise (noun /s/, verb /z/). Invisible in spelling: abuse, close, diffuse, excuse, house, use (noun /s/, verb /z/).

Fixed values (do not alternate): decrease, increase, promise, release always /s/; fuse, surprise always /z/.

Suffix rules (from the source): - -ze always /z/ (maze, seize, organize). - -ese always /iːz/ (Chinese, Portuguese). - -ism always /ɪzəm/ (capitalism, racism). - -ce always /s/ (advice, race); only desert, scissors, possess, dissolve, hussar have /z/ for ss.

See phoneme-spelling reference.

docs.title: Consonant: /ʒ/
docs.text: The voiced sibling of /ʃ/. Rare in English, and does not exist in standard Spanish. Mostly appears in -sion, -sure and French loans.

docs.title: 1. What it is
docs.text:
/ʒ/ is a voiced postalveolar fricative, the "s" in "pleasure", "vision". The voiced partner of /ʃ/.

Spanish contrast: not in standard Spanish (some regional variants have it). It is also rare in English, so it gets little practice.

docs.title: 2. How to produce it
docs.text: Exactly like /ʃ/ but with voice: tongue behind the ridge, lips rounded, vocal cords buzzing.

docs.title: 3. Angle 1 — spellings that make /ʒ/
docs.text: Spelling Examples si (in -sion after vowel) vision, decision, confusion, television su (in -sure) pleasure, measure, leisure, treasure s (in -sual/-sia) usual, casual, Asia g (French loans) genre, beige, mirage, garage (UK) z (rare) azure, seizure

docs.title: 4. Angle 2 — where the /ʒ/ sound is written (word lists)
docs.text: pleasure, exposure, vision, genre, measure, closure, leisure, equation, massage, azure, presume (variant), usual, casual, decision, confusion, television, treasure, beige, mirage.

docs.title: 5. Minimal pairs / contrasts
docs.text:
/ʒ/ rarely forms clean minimal pairs; the key contrasts are:

Pair Contrast pleasure / pressure /ʒ/ vs /ʃ/ version / virgin /ʒ/ vs /dʒ/ leisure / ledger /ʒ/ vs /dʒ/

docs.title: 6. Common Spanish error
docs.text: The trap: replacing /ʒ/ with /dʒ/ (a hard j) or /ʃ/, so "vision" gets a "ch/j" sound. The fix: it is a smooth buzzing fricative, not a stop. Same as /ʃ/ with voice. Contrast pleasure/pressure.

docs.title: Diphthongs (8 sounds)
docs.text: A diphthong is one vowel that glides into another inside a single syllable. English has 8. Spanish has diphthongs too, but the English ones differ in quality and in the glide, and the British centring diphthongs (ending in schwa) do not exist in Spanish.

docs.title: 1. What they are
docs.text:
Eight gliding vowels. Three groups:

  • Closing to /ɪ/: /eɪ/, /aɪ/, /ɔɪ/
  • Closing to /ʊ/: /aʊ/, /əʊ/
  • Centring to /ə/ (British, from a dropped R): /ɪə/, /eə/, /ʊə/

Spanish contrast: the centring diphthongs (/ɪə/, /eə/, /ʊə/) are the hard ones. They exist in SSBE because the final R is not pronounced and becomes a schwa. Spanish speakers either pronounce the R or use a pure vowel.

docs.title: 2. How to produce them
docs.text: Start on the first vowel and glide smoothly toward the second; do not break it into two syllables. For centring diphthongs, glide into a relaxed schwa and do not pronounce the R (British).

docs.title: 3. The eight diphthongs
docs.text: Diphthong As in Typical spellings Examples /eɪ/ day a-e, ai, ay, ei, ey day, stay, play, make, rate, late, great, eight, able, brain /aɪ/ try i-e, igh, y, ie try, life, like, mind, find, night, right, buy, my /ɔɪ/ boy oy, oi toy, boy, annoy, noise, join, voice /aʊ/ now ow, ou now, how, house, round, out, sound, loud, mouth /əʊ/ go o-e, oa, ow, o home, go, so, low, slow, don't, road, boat, show /ɪə/ here eer, ear, ere, ier here, ear, cheer, peer, steer, dear, deer, beer, fierce /eə/ care are, air, ear, ere there, where, care, stare, air, chair, hair, their, bear /ʊə/ tour our, ure, oor tour, cure, pure, mature, during, usually, sure, poor

docs.text:
• /eɪ/: day, stay, play, make, rate, late, great, eight, able, brain, straight, nail, pain, they, grey, veil.
  • /aɪ/: try, life, like, mind, find, night, right, buy, my, high, light, sky, die, lie.
  • /ɔɪ/: toy, boy, annoy, noise, join, voice, point, enjoy, coin, oil.
  • /aʊ/: now, how, house, round, out, sound, loud, mouth, down, town, cloud, announce, doubt, around, south, count.
  • /əʊ/: home, go, so, low, slow, don't, road, boat, show, though, although, shoulder, cold, most.
  • /ɪə/: here, ear, tear (drop), cheer, peer, steer, dear, deer, beer, fierce, idea, serious.
  • /eə/: there, where, care, stare, air, chair, hair, their, bear, area, parents, square.
  • /ʊə/: tour, cure, pure, mature, during, usually, sure, poor, Europe, jury.

docs.title: 5. Minimal pairs / contrasts
docs.text: Pair Contrast beer / bear /ɪə/ vs /eə/ here / hair /ɪə/ vs /eə/ go / saw /əʊ/ vs /ɔː/ home / ham /əʊ/ vs /æ/ by / bay /aɪ/ vs /eɪ/ so / sew(n) vs saw /əʊ/ vs /ɔː/

docs.title: 6. Common Spanish error
docs.text: The trap 1: pronouncing the written R in centring diphthongs (here, care, tour), which breaks the British sound. The trap 2: /əʊ/ said as a pure Spanish "o" (go = "gou" with Spanish o). The fix: glide into a schwa, no R (British). For /əʊ/, start from schwa, not from "o" (this is the main UK/US difference too: US uses /oʊ/).

docs.title: Double consonants
docs.text: A doubled consonant is NOT pronounced twice. It is a spelling signal: the vowel before it is short (the syllable is closed). This one insight explains a huge amount of English spelling.

docs.title: The core rule
docs.text:
A double consonant closes the preceding syllable, so the vowel is short:

Double Short vowel vs single (longer/named vowel) dinner /ɪ/ diner /aɪ/ hopping /ɒ/ hoping /əʊ/ planning /æ/ planing /eɪ/ latter /æ/ later /eɪ/ supper /ʌ/ super /uː/ bitter /ɪ/ biter /aɪ/ comma /ɒ/ coma /əʊ/

So when you see a double consonant, pronounce the consonant once and keep the vowel before it short. The doubling exists precisely to mark that short vowel.

Corollary: a single consonant between vowels often leaves the first vowel long or named (open syllable): diner, hoping, later, super.

docs.title: Double SS — voiceless, not /z/
docs.text:
A doubled consonant is also a hint about voicing. Double ss is almost always the voiceless /s/ (or /ʃ/ in -ssion), never the voiced /z/:

  • /s/: pass, miss, boss, class, kiss, mess, dress, pressure, assume.
  • /ʃ/ (in -ssion): mission, passion, discussion, expression, permission.

The handful of ss words that are /z/ are the rare exceptions: dessert, scissors, possess, dissolve, hussar. See /z/. Compare a single intervocalic s, which is frequently /z/ (easy, present, reason).

This is why "dessert" (/z/, double s but exception) vs "desert" the noun (/z/) vs "desert" the verb are confusing; the default for ss is /s/.

docs.title: Double RR — closes the syllable, dialect notes
docs.text:
Double rr also closes the syllable (short vowel before it), and it interacts with the vowel-before-r patterns:

  • arr: UK tends to a short front /æ/ (carry, marry, Harry, narrow, arrow), the same /æ/ in American. Contrast a single ar + vowel, which gives the centring /eə/ (vary, Mary, various). So carry /ˈkæri/ vs vary /ˈveəri/.
  • err: short /e/ before the doubled r (merry, berry, ferry, error, terrible).
  • irr / orr / urr: short vowel kept (mirror, sorry, horror, hurry, current).

docs.title: urr: UK /ʌr/ vs US /ɜːr/
docs.text: In a stressed closed syllable with urr, British keeps a short /ʌ/ plus r (hurry /ˈhʌri/, current, courage), while American uses the r-coloured /ɜːr/ (/ˈhɜːri/). This is the hurry-furry split.

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: Double consonants are one of the few truly systematic parts of English spelling. Reading them correctly: 1. Tells you the previous vowel is short (closed syllable). 2. Tells you ss is voiceless /s/ or /ʃ/, not /z/. 3. Tells you rr closes the syllable and shapes the a/u before r.

docs.title: Common Spanish error
docs.text: The trap: pronouncing the double consonant twice (Italian-style), or lengthening it; or voicing ss to /z/. The fix: say the consonant once, keep the vowel before it short, and keep ss voiceless.

docs.title: Grammar and usage (common Spanish errors)
docs.text: Not pronunciation, but the recurring grammar and collocation errors that Spanish speakers carry into English. Kept here so the resource covers the whole "sounds wrong" surface, not only phonetics.

docs.title: Collocation and preposition errors
docs.text: Wrong Right Note worth to + infinitive worth + gerund it's worth doing, not "worth to do" have sense make sense I am agree I agree "agree" is a verb, not an adjective responsible of responsible for people is people are "people" is plural related with related to take a decision make a decision for me (to request) to me (recipient) vs for me (benefit) distinguish any question any questions plural after "any" here

docs.title: at the end vs in the end
docs.text:
• at the end (of something) = position: "at the end of the film".
  • in the end = finally, after everything: "in the end, we agreed".

Reference: languagetool insights article (in study links).

docs.title: used to vs usually
docs.text:
• used to + infinitive = past habit no longer true: "I used to smoke".
  • usually = present habitual: "I usually walk to work".

docs.title: I / me / myself
docs.text:
• I = subject: "I did it".
  • me = object: "give it to me".
  • myself = reflexive/emphatic: "I did it myself"; not a fancy "me".

docs.text: people are, the news is, information is (uncountable), everybody is.

docs.title: Homophones
docs.text: Words spelled differently but pronounced the same. English has many, partly because of silent letters, vowel-team overlaps, and (in SSBE) non-rhoticity, which erases final-R distinctions. Useful for listening, spelling, and appreciating how far spelling drifts from sound.

docs.title: Core homophones (same in all accents)
docs.text: Set Pronunciation Notes to / too / two /tuː/ silent w in two there / their / they're /ðeə/ your / you're /jɔː/ (UK) its / it's /ɪts/ here / hear /hɪə/ know / no /nəʊ/ silent k knight / night /naɪt/ silent k, gh write / right / rite /raɪt/ silent w, gh hour / our /aʊə/ silent h hole / whole /həʊl/ silent w in whole sea / see /siː/ meet / meat /miːt/ peace / piece /piːs/ flour / flower /flaʊə/ sun / son /sʌn/ one / won /wʌn/ buy / by / bye /baɪ/ cell / sell /sel/ soft c cent / scent / sent /sent/ silent c in scent break / brake /breɪk/ plain / plane /pleɪn/ whether / weather /ˈweðə/ silent h in whether which / witch /wɪtʃ/ allowed / aloud /əˈlaʊd/ bored / board /bɔːd/ pair / pear / pare /peə/ waist / waste /weɪst/

docs.title: Non-rhotic (British) homophones
docs.text:
In SSBE the final R is not pronounced, so these merge in British English but usually stay distinct in rhotic American:

Set SSBE pronunciation Distinct in US? paw / pour / poor /pɔː/ (for many speakers) yes saw / sore / soar /sɔː/ yes court / caught /kɔːt/ yes father / farther /ˈfɑːðə/ yes formally / formerly /ˈfɔːməli/ yes wander / wonder close, not exact —

docs.title: Accent-dependent near-homophones (yod coalescence)
docs.text:
In relaxed SSBE, /dj/ and /tj/ coalesce to /dʒ/ and /tʃ/, which merges some words that are distinct in careful speech:

Set Careful Coalesced (casual SSBE) dual / duel / jewel /ˈdjuːəl/, /ˈdjuːəl/, /ˈdʒuːəl/ all -> /ˈdʒuːəl/ due / dew / Jew /djuː/, /djuː/, /dʒuː/ due/dew -> /dʒuː/ = Jew tune / (a) choon /tjuːn/ -> /tʃuːn/

So "dual", "duel" and "jewel" can all sound identical in casual British speech, even though "jewel" starts from a different spelling. This is yod coalescence, the same process that gives nature /ˈneɪtʃə/ and education /edʒuˈkeɪʃn/. See connected speech and the letter U.

docs.title: Why so many homophones
docs.text:
• Silent letters collapse distinctions: know/no, hour/our, write/right.
  • Vowel teams overlap: meet/meat, sea/see, plain/plane.
  • Non-rhoticity (SSBE) erases final-R contrasts: paw/pour, saw/sore.
  • Yod coalescence merges /dj, tj/ pairs in casual speech: dual/jewel.

docs.text: Not an error so much as a listening and spelling challenge: a single sound can map to several spellings. Context disambiguates in speech; spelling must be learned per word.

docs.title: Intonation
docs.text: Intonation, the melody of speech, carries meaning in English. The same words can be a statement, a question, or a signal of attitude depending on the pitch pattern.

docs.title: 1. Why it matters
docs.text: English uses pitch to signal grammar and attitude, not just emotion. Wrong intonation can turn a statement into a question, sound rude, or obscure the point. Spanish uses intonation too, but the patterns differ, and English leans on it more heavily because it is stress-timed.

docs.title: 2. Thought groups
docs.text:
Speech is chunked into thought groups: short meaningful phrases separated by tiny pauses. Each group has one main stressed word (the nucleus) that carries the pitch movement.

Chunking correctly makes long sentences intelligible: "When I got home // I realised // I had left my keys // at the office."

docs.title: 3. The main tunes
docs.text:
• Falling tone: statements, commands, wh-questions, finished thoughts. "I live in Madrid." (pitch falls on MA-drid)
  • Rising tone: yes/no questions, uncertainty, "please continue". "Are you coming?" (pitch rises at the end)
  • Fall-rise: contrast, reservation, politeness. "I LIKE it..." (but).

docs.title: 4. Nucleus placement
docs.text: The most important word in a thought group gets the pitch movement. Moving the nucleus changes meaning: - "I didn't say she STOLE it." (someone else did / she did something else) - The stressed word signals the focus.

docs.title: 5. Uptalk
docs.text: The rising tone on statements (high rising terminal). Common in some accents and younger speakers. Worth recognising; use with care.

docs.title: 6. Common Spanish error
docs.text: The trap: flat or Spanish-pattern intonation, or rising where English falls, making statements sound like questions. The fix: chunk into thought groups, put the pitch movement on the key word, and fall at the end of statements and wh-questions.

docs.title: The letter A (two angles)
docs.text: The key skill is to look at the letter A from both directions: given the written 'a', which sound; given a phoneme, which spellings produce it. The letter U gets the same treatment in spelling-to-sound rules.

docs.title: Angle 1 — how a written 'a' is pronounced
docs.text:
Context Sound Examples Closed syllable /æ/ cat, bad, trap, hat, apple, random Open syllable / Magic e /eɪ/ (alphabet a) make, rate, late, able, basic, nation a + R (stressed) /ɑː/ (UK); /ɑːr/ (US) car, start, far, hard, park a + R + e / a + ir /eə/ (UK); /er/ (US) care, fair, chair, air, stare a before l (often) /ɔː/ call, tall, walk, talk, salt, false a + W / a + U /ɔː/ law, saw, cause, author, launch Unstressed /ə/ schwa banana, about, alarm, america, academy Many words (UK only) /ɑː/ long a past, path, class, last, fast, bath

TRAP-BATH split: words like past, path, class, last, dance take long /ɑː/ in SSBE but /æ/ in General American. This is the single biggest UK/US difference for the letter A.

docs.title: Angle 2 — where the /æ/ sound is written
docs.text:
Almost always a written 'a' in a closed syllable:

cat, bad, trap, hat, man, map, cash, back, apple, random, contract, impact, diagram, transition, artifact, blackboard, abstract.

Note (UK): some closed-'a' words move to /ɑː/ instead (past, path, class). In American they stay /æ/.

docs.title: Angle 2 — where the /ɑː/ (long a) sound is written
docs.text: Spelling Examples a + R car, start, far, hard, park, large, March a (UK TRAP-BATH) past, path, class, last, fast, bath, dance, chance al + consonant (silent l) calm, palm, half, calf foreign / misc father, drama, banana (final), tomato (UK)

docs.title: The letters OU (two angles)
docs.text: OU is the most unstable vowel team in English: around 11 different pronunciations. There is no single rule; each word is learned. This page lists them both ways so the patterns are at least visible.

docs.title: Angle 1 — how written 'ou' is pronounced (all 11)
docs.text: Sound Examples /ʌ/ enough, young, couple, touch, rough, encourage, country /ɒ/ cough, trough /ɔː/ course, court, four, source, your, board, bought, brought, ought, thought /ʊ/ could, should, would /uː/ group, soup, route, through /ɜː/ journey, journal /ə/ famous, nervous, dangerous (unstressed -ous) /aʊ/ sound, house, loud, mount, mouse, out, announce, doubt, around, south, count /əʊ/ although, shoulder, soul, dough /ʊə/ tour /aʊə/ our, hour, flour, sour (ou + r)

docs.title: Angle 2 — grouping by the resulting sound
docs.text:
• Most common everyday value is /aʊ/ (out, house, sound).
  • Before -ght, OU is almost always /ɔː/ (thought, bought, ought).
  • -ous suffix is always the weak /ə/ (famous, dangerous, nervous).
  • A small fixed set is /ʊ/: could, should, would.
  • Function/short words vary: you /uː/, your /ɔː/, young /ʌ/.

docs.title: Practical approach
docs.text:
1. Learn the fixed subsets: -ought/-ought = /ɔː/; -ous = /ə/; could/should/ would = /ʊ/.
  2. Default an unknown stressed OU to /aʊ/ (out, house), the most frequent.
  3. Memorise the /ʌ/ group (enough, young, touch, country), a common trap for Spanish speakers who say /u/.

docs.title: Common Spanish error
docs.text: The trap: reading OU as a Spanish "ou"/"u", so "country" = "coun-tri" with /u/, or "enough" with /u/. The fix: there is no single value. Learn the subsets above; the /ʌ/ group (enough, young, couple, touch, country) is the highest-value fix.

docs.title: The letter U (two angles)
docs.text: Like the letter A, the written U is highly predictable once you read it both ways: given the spelling, which sound; given the sound, which spelling.

docs.title: Angle 1 — how a written 'u' is pronounced
docs.text: Context Sound Examples Notes Closed syllable /ʌ/ cut, much, judge, luxury, under, sudden ~99% of cases Closed exceptions /ʊ/ put, push, bull, pull, bullet, full learn these Open syllable / Magic e /juː/ or /uː/ cube, cute, duke, tune, tube, presume, during US often drops yod u + R (stressed) /ɜː/ long schwa turn, purge, curve, further, turtle always, barring exceptions Unstressed /ə/ or /ʊ/ exposure, measure, culture

docs.title: Unwritten rule — yod drop after L or R
docs.text:
Open-syllable/magic-e U is /juː/, but the yod /j/ drops after L or R, even in British English.

Word Expected Actual Why conclusion /kluː.../ with yod no yod open syllable, L before include yod no yod L before rude yod no yod R before blue yod no yod L before

Americans drop the yod far more widely (tune, duke, due, student, news).

docs.title: Precise yod distribution (from the source)
docs.text:
/j/ appears before /uː/ and /ʊə/ when the sound is spelled u, ue, eu, ew, ure, and is NOT preceded by j, ch, r, or consonant+l: - With yod: tube, duty, music, fuel, due, cue, Tuesday, feud, neutral, ewe, few, new, mural, euro, pure, mature. - Without yod: Jew, June, juice, chew, chute, rude, crew, prune, blue, plural, sluice.

Optional yod (may be dropped, especially after θ, s, z, l): suit, sewage, lute, absolute, revolution, salute, enthusiasm.

docs.title: Angle 2 — where /juː/ (and yod-drop /uː/) is written
docs.text:
Full yod candidate list (UK keeps most; US drops many; both drop after L/R):

actual, natural, virtual, eventual, perpetual, situation, mutual, mature, youtube, tuesday, stupid, tune, tutorial, attitude, opportunity, gradual, individual, procedure, education, schedule, module, during, duplex, duke, due, deduce, reduce, produce, accurate, security, documentation, communicate, formula, emulate, mutate, museum, argue, regulate, singular, annual, tenure, nuke, manual, computer, pure, putrefaction, stipulate, tribune, albumen, distribute, beauty, future.

docs.title: Angle 2 — where /ʌ/ (closed u) is written
docs.text:
cut, much, judge, luxury, under, sudden, public, publish, bubble, up, cut, redundancy, concurrent, fun, sunday, drunk, pulse, assumption, summary, sublimate, ugly, fluctuate.

Exceptions that take /ʊ/ instead: put, push, bull, pull, full, bullet.

docs.title: Common Spanish error
docs.text: The trap: pronouncing u+R as /ʌ/ (as if closed), so "turn" = "tun"; or keeping the yod where it drops (rude with a yod). The fix: stressed u+R is always long schwa /ɜː/. Drop the yod after L and R.

docs.title: Long /ɑː/ word families (UK TRAP-BATH)
docs.text:
In SSBE, a large set of words spelled with "a" take the long back /ɑː/ where American keeps the short front /æ/. This is the TRAP-BATH split. The words group neatly by the consonant(s) that follow the "a".

See /ɑː/ (back a) for the sound itself.

docs.title: Why group by the following consonant
docs.text: The split is not random: SSBE lengthened "a" to /ɑː/ mainly before certain consonant environments, voiceless fricatives (/f/, /θ/, /s/) and some nasal clusters. Grouping by what follows makes the pattern learnable.

docs.title: a + S sounds (/s/, /ss/, /st/, /sk/, /sp/)
docs.text: grass, class, glass, pass, brass, last, fast, past, cast, vast, mast, blast, ask, task, mask, basket, rascal, grasp, clasp, plaster, master, disaster.

docs.title: a + TH (/θ/)
docs.text: bath, path, lath, aftermath. (Not "math" in American; UK says /bɑːθ/.)

docs.title: a + F (/f/)
docs.text: after, craft, draft, graft, shaft, raft, staff, laugh (gh = /f/), daft.

docs.title: a + N + consonant (/ns/, /nt/, /ntʃ/, /nd/, /ntʃ/)
docs.text: dance, chance, France, glance, advance, prance, branch, ranch, command, demand, grant, plant, slant, answer, example, sample, can't, shan't.

docs.title: a + R (always /ɑː/, both UK and US core)
docs.text: car, far, start, hard, park, large, March, garden, market, argue, guard, charge, sharp, part, art, card. (This group is /ɑː/ in both accents; R-colour in American.)

docs.title: al with silent l (/ɑː/)
docs.text: calm, palm, half, calf, almond. (The l is silent; see silent letters.)

docs.title: Misc / foreign
docs.text: father, drama, pasta (UK), banana (final a), tomato (UK), vase (UK).

docs.title: What stays short /æ/ (does NOT join the split)
docs.text: Many a-words keep /æ/ even in SSBE: cat, bad, trap, man, map, back, flat, hand, land, stand, random, gas, pan, bank, cash. The split is specific to the environments above, and even then has exceptions (e.g. "mass", "gas", "lass" stay /æ/; "ant", "romance" vary).

docs.title: Practice tip
docs.text: When you meet a new a-word in these environments, default to /ɑː/ for SSBE and /æ/ for American. For "-ance/-ant" the split is less consistent, so check.

docs.title: Common Spanish error
docs.text: The trap: using one short, front, Spanish "a" everywhere, missing the long back /ɑː/ entirely. The fix: learn the families above as sets. The S/TH/F groups are the most consistent; master those first.

docs.title: Minimal pairs
docs.text: Pairs of words that differ in exactly one phoneme. They are where Spanish speakers lose intelligibility, and the best drill for fixing a specific contrast. Grouped by the contrast being trained.

docs.title: /ɪ/ vs /iː/ (short vs long i)
docs.text: ship/sheep, bit/beat, live/leave, sit/seat, fit/feet, rich/reach, it/eat, fill/feel.

docs.title: /æ/ vs /ʌ/ (front a vs hat a)
docs.text: cat/cut, cap/cup, ran/run, bat/but, match/much.

docs.title: /æ/ vs /e/
docs.text: bad/bed, bat/bet, sad/said, man/men, had/head.

docs.title: /e/ vs /ɪ/
docs.text: bed/bid, pen/pin, ten/tin, desk/disk.

docs.title: /ʌ/ vs /ɒ/
docs.text: luck/lock, cut/cot, nut/not, duck/dock.

docs.title: /ɒ/ vs /ɔː/
docs.text: cot/caught, pot/port, not/nought, spot/sport.

docs.title: /ʊ/ vs /uː/
docs.text: full/fool, pull/pool, look/Luke, could/cooed.

docs.title: /ɑː/ vs /ʌ/ and /ɜː/
docs.text: cart/cut, calm/come, heart/hurt, far/fur, stir/star.

docs.title: Diphthong contrasts
docs.text: beer/bear (/ɪə/-/eə/), here/hair, go/saw (/əʊ/-/ɔː/), by/bay (/aɪ/-/eɪ/).

docs.text: berry/very, ban/van, best/vest, boat/vote, curb/curve, bowel/vowel.

docs.text: ice/eyes, price/prize, bus/buzz, face/phase, loose/lose, racer/razor.

docs.text: she/see, ship/sip, sheet/seat, shave/save, sham/Sam.

docs.text: share/chair, sheep/cheap, shop/chop, cash/catch, shoes/choose.

docs.title: /θ/ vs /s/ and /t/
docs.text: think/sink, thing/sing, mouth/mouse; thin/tin, three/tree, bath/bat.

docs.title: /ŋ/ vs /n/

docs.title: Practice
docs.text: Use pairs as a daily drill: say both, exaggerate the contrast, then use each in a short sentence. See study links for minimal-pair quizzes (Marcus) and exercises (hot/hat, cheese/cheat).

docs.title: More spelling rules (and negative rules)
docs.text: Additional reliable patterns, plus "negative rules" (what a letter never does). Negative rules are high-value for Spanish speakers because they eliminate a whole class of errors at once.

docs.title: A written "c" is NEVER /z/
docs.text:
English "c" is only: - hard /k/ before a, o, u, or a consonant: cat, cot, cut, clock, cream. - soft /s/ before e, i, y: city, cent, cycle, precise, decide, receive.

It is never /z/ and never /θ/ in standard English. So "precise", "decision", "city" have /s/. A common Spanish pitfall is voicing it; do not.

docs.title: A stressed written "a" is NEVER /ʌ/
docs.text: A written "a" in a stressed syllable is never the /ʌ/ of "cut". It is usually the front /æ/ (cat), and can also be /eɪ/ (cake), /ɑː/ (car, past), /ɔː/ (call, water), /ɒ/ (want, wash), or /eə/ (care) — but never /ʌ/. The /ʌ/ sound is spelled u, o, or ou (cut, love, touch), not a. So never read "cat" as "cut".

docs.title: Other quick negatives
docs.text:
• A single written "s" at the start of a word is /s/, never /z/ (so, sun, send). Initial /z/ is spelled z (zoo).
  • "ss" is /s/ or /ʃ/, never /z/ (except dessert, scissors, possess, dissolve, hussar). See double consonants.
  • "ph" is /f/, never /p/+/h/.

docs.title: Vowel teams are almost never read literally
docs.text: Two written vowels (a vowel team) are almost never pronounced as the two Spanish vowels in sequence. ai is not "a-i", ea is not "e-a", oa is not "o-a". A team usually spells ONE sound, either a long vowel or a diphthong.

docs.title: Teams that resemble their spelling (the partial exceptions)
docs.text:
These glide diphthongs do roughly track the letters, because the sound glides from the first vowel toward the second:

Team Sound Examples ay, ai, ey /eɪ/ day, rain, survey, they, obey oy, oi /ɔɪ/ boy, boil, enjoy ou, ow /aʊ/ house, now, loud

docs.title: The /əʊ/ trap (British vs American)
docs.text: The go/home vowel is NOT "o-u". In British English it is /əʊ/ = schwa + ʊ (go, home, though, road, show). Americans use /oʊ/, which is closer to the spelling. Spanish speakers must not read it as a Spanish "o" or "ou".

docs.title: Second value: unstressed ey/ay -> /i/
docs.text: When unstressed and final, ey/ay weaken to /i/ (not /eɪ/): money, honey, monkey, journey, Sunday, Monday, holiday.

docs.title: EI — the showcase irregular team
docs.text:
"ei" is the clearest proof that teams are not read literally. It has at least five values and no reliable rule; each word is learned:

Sound Examples Note /eɪ/ vein, veil, rein, reign, feign, eight, weight, neighbour, sleigh, freight the "they" vowel /iː/ receive, deceive, conceive, perceive, ceiling, seize, protein, caffeine long i; surprises Spanish speakers; "i before e except after c" /aɪ/ height, sleight, Einstein, feisty, heist; either/neither (UK) the "my" diphthong /e/ heifer, leisure (UK), Leicester short e /ə/ or /ɪ/ foreign, forfeit, surfeit, counterfeit, sovereign weak, unstressed

Note the spelling distinction: "ey" (survey, they, money) and "ei" (vein, receive, height) behave differently; do not conflate them. The biggest trap in "ei" is the long /iː/ group (receive, ceiling, protein), which looks nothing like its sound.

docs.title: The letter X
docs.text: Written "x" has three values; the first two are rule-governed.

docs.title: Default: /ks/
docs.text: Most of the time x is /ks/: box, tax, relax, fix, six, exit (variant), expect, extra, exercise, excellent, expert, complex, text, next.

docs.title: /gz/ — before a stressed vowel-initial syllable
docs.text:
X becomes /gz/ (the voiced counterpart) when it sits immediately before a stressed syllable that begins with a vowel sound:

exámple, exáct, exám, exémption, exíst, exháust (h is silent -> vowel), exótic, exággerate, exécutive, exémplary, exúberant.

docs.title: Two things block /gz/ (so it stays /ks/)
docs.text:
1. Stress is NOT on the following syllable. If the stress is before the x, it stays /ks/: éxercise, éxcellent, éxpert, éxhale (variant), éxecute.
  2. The following sound is a consonant, not a vowel. The syllable after x then starts with a consonant, so /gz/ cannot apply:
  3. exc- (c = /s/): exception, excite, excel, exceed, excellent. "exc-" is always /ks/ even when stress follows (excéption), because of the c.
  4. exp-: expect, explain, express, expand.
  5. ext-: extend, extreme, extract.
  6. excl-/expl-: exclude, explode.

So exception is /ɪkˈsep.../ (ks) while example is /ɪgˈzɑːm.../ (gz): both have the stress after the x, but exception's next sound is the consonant /s/.

docs.title: Word-initial x -> /z/
docs.text: At the start of a word, x is /z/, never /ks/: xylophone, xerox, xenon, xenophobia, Xena.

docs.title: Edge cases
docs.text:
• exit: /ˈeksɪt/ or /ˈegzɪt/ (both heard).
  • luxury /ˈlʌkʃəri/ (ks -> kʃ) vs luxurious /lʌgˈʒʊəriəs/ (gz -> gʒ): same stress-driven voicing, palatalised before the yod.
  • Final -x and most clusters stay /ks/: six, box, complexion, anxious (/ŋkʃ/).

docs.title: Soft vs hard C and G
docs.text:
Letter Before e, i, y Before a, o, u / consonant c soft /s/: city, cent, cycle hard /k/: cat, cot, cut, clip g soft /dʒ/ (usually): gym, giant, gentle hard /g/: go, gap, gun, glad

G is less regular than c: some words keep hard /g/ before e/i (get, give, girl, gift, begin, tiger). C is highly regular.

docs.title: -AL tends to /ɔːl/
docs.text:
Before a consonant and word-finally, "al" often becomes /ɔːl/ (the l is a dark l): call, tall, wall, fall, hall, ball, small, always, also, although, salt, halt, false, bald, walk, talk, chalk (these last three with silent l -> /ɔːk/).

But this is a tendency, not a law. Exceptions keep /æl/: shall, pal, alley, valley, balance, talent, salad, canal (final stress), Alabama. And "al" + vowel is usually /æl/ (alien is /eɪ/; value /æl/).

Takeaway: "al + consonant" leans strongly to /ɔːl/; "al + vowel" usually stays /æl/.

docs.title: Intervocalic a + r -> /eə/ (vary, Mary, parent)
docs.text:
When a stressed "a" is followed by a single r plus another vowel, it is the centring /eə/ (UK adds a mini schwa before the r), not /æ/ or /ɑː/:

vary, various, variable, Mary, scary, canary, aquarium, parent, area, rarity, Sarah, wary, library (first a).

Contrast with a doubled rr, which closes the syllable and gives short /æ/: carry, marry, Harry, narrow. So vary /ˈveəri/ vs carry /ˈkæri/. See double consonants.

The same single-r-before-vowel pattern gives /ɪə/ for "e/i" (hero, serious, Vera, query, period) and /ʊə/ / /jʊə/ for "u" (fury, curious, Europe).

docs.title: -OUGH (the seven-way spelling)
docs.text:
"ough" is the most irregular string in English:

Sound Examples /ɔː/ thought, bought, ought, sought, nought /əʊ/ though, dough, although /uː/ through /ʌf/ enough, rough, tough /ɒf/ cough, trough /aʊ/ bough, plough, drought /ə/ borough, thorough (UK)

No rule; each must be learned. Listed here so the trap is visible.

docs.title: Y as a vowel
docs.text:
• Stressed, final or alone: /aɪ/ — my, cry, by, try, type, cycle.
  • Unstressed, final: /i/ (close to /ɪ/) — happy, city, funny, quickly.
  • Medial: /ɪ/ — gym, system, myth, crystal.

docs.title: GH
docs.text:
• Silent: light, night, though, through, daughter, high.
  • /f/: enough, rough, tough, cough, laugh (the -ough/-augh set).
  • Never a hard /g/+/h/.

docs.title: Common Spanish error
docs.text: The trap: voicing c to /z/, reading stressed "a" as /ʌ/, or reading "al" as a plain /al/. The fix: internalise the negatives (c never /z/; stressed a never /ʌ/) and the al -> /ɔːl/ tendency. They remove whole error classes.

docs.title: Noun/verb pairs (same spelling, different pronunciation)
docs.text:
Many English words are spelled identically as a noun/adjective and as a verb but pronounced differently. The difference is one of two mechanisms: a STRESS SHIFT (which also reduces the unstressed vowel), or a SOUND CHANGE (a consonant or vowel changes) with no stress shift. Classify each pair; do not assume they all shift.

Summary table also lives on word stress; this page is the full treatment.

docs.title: The two mechanisms
docs.text:
1. Stress shift: the stress moves between syllables, and the now-unstressed syllable reduces to schwa. Example: REcord /ˈrekɔːd/ (noun) vs reCORD /rɪˈkɔːd/ (verb), the first vowel goes from /e/ to /ɪ/ (reduced).
  2. Sound change without stress shift: a consonant voices or a vowel changes, but the stress stays. Example: use /juːs/ (noun) vs use /juːz/ (verb).

docs.title: Class A — Standard shifters (noun/adjective 1st, verb 2nd)
docs.text:
The classic set. Noun/adjective stresses syllable 1; verb stresses syllable 2. The unstressed syllable reduces, so the vowels differ too.

Word Noun/adj (1st) Verb (2nd) record REcord reCORD present PREsent preSENT contract CONtract conTRACT progress PROgress proGRESS export EXport exPORT import IMport imPORT rebel REbel reBEL permit PERmit perMIT conduct CONduct conDUCT object OBject obJECT subject SUBject subJECT insult INsult inSULT suspect SUSpect susPECT contrast CONtrast conTRAST increase INcrease inCREASE decrease DEcrease deCREASE protest PROtest proTEST discount DIScount disCOUNT upgrade UPgrade upGRADE conflict CONflict conFLICT convert CONvert conVERT transport TRANSport transPORT address ADdress (US) adDRESS refund REfund reFUND

docs.title: Class B — Always first syllable (no shift)
docs.text:
Both noun and verb stress syllable 1; no change. Many have the stress-neutral -ment ending or are simply fixed.

comment, promise, focus, profit, picture, visit, answer, programme, process (UK), travel, label, offer, order, murder, promise, purchase, witness, comfort, credit, limit, benefit, balance, damage.

Note on endings: the -ment noun suffix is stress-neutral (COMment, GOVernment, ARGument), which is why "comment" stays on the first syllable. But -ent in general is NOT always unstressed, many words stress it (eVENT, preVENT, reSENT, inVENT, perCENT), so do not over-generalise from -ment.

docs.title: Class C — Always second syllable (no shift)
docs.text:
Both noun and verb stress syllable 2; no change.

report, request, result, release, respect, review, reward, surprise, concern, mistake, control, command, demand, support, account, debate, delay, design, dislike, escape, exchange, reply, research (UK also REsearch).

docs.title: Class D — Sound change (not stress) and irregular pairs
docs.text: Here the pronunciation changes but the stress usually does NOT move. Often a voicing change (see the /s/-/z/ alternation) or a vowel change.

docs.title: Voicing: noun/adjective /s/ vs verb /z/
docs.text:
The final /s/ voices to /z/ in the verb; stress unchanged.

Word Noun/adj /s/ Verb /z/ use /juːs/ /juːz/ house /haʊs/ /haʊz/ close /kləʊs/ (adj) /kləʊz/ abuse /əˈbjuːs/ /əˈbjuːz/ excuse /ɪkˈskjuːs/ /ɪkˈskjuːz/ diffuse /dɪˈfjuːs/ (adj) /dɪˈfjuːz/ misuse /ˌmɪsˈjuːs/ /ˌmɪsˈjuːz/ grease /griːs/ /griːz/ (variable)

Spelled to mark it: advice/advise, device/devise, licence/license (UK), practice/practise (UK). See the /s/-/z/ alternation.

docs.title: Voicing: noun /θ/ vs verb /ð/
docs.text:
The spelling often marks it: -th noun, -the verb. Several also change the vowel.

Noun /θ/ Verb /ð/ bath /bɑːθ/ bathe /beɪð/ (vowel change too) breath /breθ/ breathe /briːð/ (vowel change too) cloth /klɒθ/ clothe /kləʊð/ (vowel change too) teeth /tiːθ/ teethe /tiːð/ sheath /ʃiːθ/ sheathe /ʃiːð/ wreath /riːθ/ wreathe /riːð/ mouth /maʊθ/ mouth (verb) /maʊð/ loath /ləʊθ/ (adj) loathe /ləʊð/

See /θ/, /ð/.

docs.title: Voicing: noun /f/ vs verb /v/
docs.text:
Often spelled -f (noun) / -ve (verb):

Noun /f/ Verb /v/ shelf shelve half halve grief grieve belief believe relief relieve proof prove thief thieve safe (adj) save strife strive (vowel shift too)

docs.title: Vowel change (no voicing, no stress shift)
docs.text:
The -ate family: adjective/noun /ət/, verb /eɪt/, stress unchanged.

Word Noun/adj Verb separate /ˈseprət/ /ˈsepəreɪt/ estimate /ˈestɪmət/ /ˈestɪmeɪt/ graduate /ˈgrædʒuət/ /ˈgrædʒueɪt/ moderate /ˈmɒdərət/ /ˈmɒdəreɪt/ deliberate /dɪˈlɪbərət/ /dɪˈlɪbəreɪt/ delegate /ˈdelɪgət/ /ˈdelɪgeɪt/ advocate /ˈædvəkət/ /ˈædvəkeɪt/ duplicate /ˈdjuːplɪkət/ /ˈdjuːplɪkeɪt/

Plus: live, adjective /laɪv/ vs verb /lɪv/.

docs.title: Heteronyms (same spelling, different word/sense, different sound)
docs.text:
These are NOT strictly noun-vs-verb; they are same-spelled words with unrelated senses and different pronunciations. Listed because they belong to the same "spelling lies" phenomenon.

Word Reading 1 Reading 2 lead /liːd/ (to guide, verb) /led/ (the metal, noun) read /riːd/ (present) /red/ (past) wind /wɪnd/ (air, noun) /waɪnd/ (to turn, verb) tear /tɪə/ (crying, noun) /teə/ (to rip, verb) bow /bəʊ/ (ribbon/weapon) /baʊ/ (to bend) minute /ˈmɪnɪt/ (time, noun) /maɪˈnjuːt/ (tiny, adj) row /rəʊ/ (line / to row) /raʊ/ (a quarrel) close /kləʊs/ (near, adj) /kləʊz/ (to shut, verb) content /ˈkɒntent/ (what's inside, noun) /kənˈtent/ (satisfied, adj)

Some heteronyms (content, close) overlap with the earlier classes; they are repeated here to show the full "one spelling, two sounds" set.

docs.title: How to decide
docs.text:
1. Is it in the standard shifter set (Class A)? Then noun -> 1st, verb -> 2nd, and reduce the unstressed syllable.
  2. If not, check whether it is a fixed first (Class B) or second (Class C) word, no change.
  3. Watch for the sound-change pairs (Class D): use/use, house/house, separate, bath/bathe, where the stress stays but a sound changes.

docs.title: Common Spanish error
docs.text: The trap: using one pronunciation for both the noun and the verb, or assuming every same-spelled pair shifts stress. The fix: learn the standard shifter set (record, present, contract), and treat the sound-change pairs (use, house, close, separate) separately, their stress does not move.

/θ/ - /ð/ alternation (noun vs verb)
docs.text:
Spelling signals it: nouns end -th (voiceless /θ/), verbs end -the (voiced /ð/).

Noun /θ/ Verb /ð/ bath bathe breath breathe sheath sheathe teeth teethe wreath wreathe

Also north/northern, south/southern, worth/worthy use /θ/ -> /ð/. Position rules: initial th in function words is /ð/ (the, this, then), but content words are /θ/ (think, through); medial th + -er/-ing is usually /ð/ (other, bathing) with exceptions (panther, ether, anything). See /θ/ and /ð/.

docs.title: /s/ - /z/ alternation (noun vs verb)
docs.text:
Final -se can be /s/ or /z/; some pairs are spelled to mark it:

Noun /s/ Verb /z/ advice advise device devise licence (UK noun) license (UK verb) practice (UK noun) practise (UK verb)

Invisible in spelling: abuse, close, diffuse, excuse, house, use (noun /s/, verb /z/). Fixed: decrease, increase, promise, release always /s/; fuse, surprise always /z/. See /s/ vs /z/.

docs.title: Yod (/j/) distribution
docs.text:
/j/ appears before /uː/ and /ʊə/ when spelled u, ue, eu, ew, ure, and NOT preceded by j, ch, r, or consonant+l.

  • With yod: tube, duty, music, fuel, due, cue, Tuesday, feud, neutral, ewe, few, new, mural, euro, pure, mature.
  • Without yod (dropped): Jew, June, juice, chew, chute, rude, crew, prune, blue, plural, sluice.

The two-syllable /ɪə/ often compresses to /jə/ (audience, idiot, India); /uə/ to /wə/ (usual, innocuous). See the letter U and long u /uː/.

docs.title: Priority phonemes for Spanish speakers
docs.text: Not all phonemes matter equally. These are the highest-leverage ones for a native Spanish speaker, in order.

docs.title: Vowels (top 4)
docs.text:
1. Schwa /ə/. The most important. The biggest Spanish error is not using it; Spanish forces a full written vowel into every syllable. Even schwa deletion never happens in Spanish speech. See schwa.
  2. Long schwa /ɜː/. Very specific sound; almost no Spanish native says it right. Appears in many common words. Spelled via vowel + R patterns: I+R, U+R, E+R, W+OR (and a few others). Knowing the spelling-to-sound mapping both ways is key.
  3. Short /ɪ/. Does not exist in Spanish. The issue is quality, not length versus /iː/. No Spanish speaker pronounces it well. Many common minimal pairs with /iː/ make it critical (leave/live, cheese/cheat).
  4. Long back /ɑː/. The genuinely hard one for Spanish speakers, not the front /æ/. The Spanish "a" is fairly front, so /æ/ (cat) is close enough; the long, back /ɑː/ (car, father, past) is the foreign sound. More frequent in SSBE than in American because of the TRAP-BATH split (past, path, class take /ɑː/ in SSBE, /æ/ in American). Spanish speakers also tend to add a rolled R in words like "car".

Note: in SSBE the long/short vowel distinction is more elastic (more evident) than in American. IPA often marks the two dots (ː) for British and drops them for American.

docs.title: Consonants (most important, do not exist in Spanish)
docs.text:
1. R. Very different from the Spanish R; almost no native produces the English R well.
  2. Dark L. Distorts adjacent sounds and phonemes heavily. Spanish speakers rarely produce it.
  3. /z/. Does not exist in Spanish. Many S/Z minimal pairs.
  4. /ʃ/ (SH). Very common. We can produce it, but the problem is not knowing which spellings trigger it (not only written SH; many endings).
  5. /v/. Does not exist in Spanish; "b" and "v" are the same letter-sound, so speakers collapse /b/ and /v/. Many minimal pairs (berry/very, ban/van, best/vest). A distinct labiodental, not a bilabial.
  6. H. Spanish speakers tend to say it like a Spanish J or drop it entirely.

The rest of the non-Spanish consonants matter but are lower priority. /tʃ/ (CH) exists in some Spanish regions (Río de la Plata, parts of Spain), so it is producible; its voiced sibling /ʒ/ is much rarer in English.

docs.title: R and W break the vowel rules
docs.text: Two letters systematically distort the normal spelling-to-sound rules: R and W. They change the vowel that comes with them, so the usual syllable rules (closed = short, etc.) do not apply. This confuses Spanish speakers badly, because the spelling looks regular but the sound is not.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
The syllable rules predict vowels well, UNTIL an R or a W is involved. Then: - R colours and usually lengthens the preceding vowel; vowel+r rarely sounds like the plain vowel. - W rounds or backs a following a, and flips some r-combinations.

Learn these as overrides to the normal rules.

docs.title: u + r -> /ɜː/ (not the closed /ʌ/)
docs.text:
A u in a closed syllable is normally /ʌ/ (cut, bus, sun). But u + r flips it to the long schwa /ɜː/, not /ʌ/ + r:

cut /ʌ/ -> curt /ɜː/; bun -> burn; cub -> curb; hut -> hurt; tun -> turn. Also: nurse, purse, curse, church, further, turtle, disturb, Thursday.

So the closed-syllable rule is overridden by the r. This is a top Spanish trap: they say turn as "turn" with /ʌ/ + a rolled r.

docs.title: vowel + r in general (r-controlled syllables)
docs.text: Every vowel changes before r: - a + r -> /ɑː/ (car, start), but a + r + e -> /eə/ (care), and intervocalic a + r -> /eə/ (vary); see more spelling rules. - e/i/u + r (stressed) -> /ɜː/ (her, bird, turn). - o + r -> /ɔː/ (short, born). See each vowel page and long schwa /ɜː/.

docs.title: double rr closes the syllable
docs.text: arr -> short /æ/ (carry) vs single ar + vowel -> /eə/ (vary); urr -> UK /ʌr/ (hurry) vs US /ɜːr/. Full detail in double consonants.

docs.title: w + a -> /ɒ/ (not /æ/)
docs.text:
After w (and qu), a written a is rounded to /ɒ/, not the expected front /æ/:

want, wash, watch, swan, swamp, wander, what; quality, quantity, squad, quarrel, quarantine. Compare "cat" /æ/ with "watch" /ɒ/.

docs.title: w + or -> /ɜː/ (not /ɔː/)
docs.text:
"or" is normally /ɔː/ (for, short, born). After w it becomes /ɜː/:

work, word, world, worm, worse, worth, worship. Exceptions keep /ɔː/: worn, sworn.

docs.title: w + ar -> /ɔː/ (not /ɑː/)
docs.text:
"ar" is normally /ɑː/ (car, far). After w it becomes /ɔː/:

war, warm, ward, warn, dwarf, reward, quarter, towards.

So w pulls the vowel one way (a -> /ɒ/, ar -> /ɔː/, or -> /ɜː/); none follow the plain rule.

docs.title: Summary table
docs.text: Sequence Normal rule With R/W override Examples u (closed) /ʌ/ u + r -> /ɜː/ cut vs curt, turn, burn a /æ/ w/qu + a -> /ɒ/ cat vs watch, want, squad ar /ɑː/ w + ar -> /ɔː/ car vs war, warm, ward or /ɔː/ w + or -> /ɜː/ for vs work, word, world

docs.title: Common Spanish error
docs.text: The trap: applying the normal syllable rule and reading turn as /tʌrn/, watch as /wætʃ/, or work as /wɔːrk/, usually with a rolled Spanish r. The fix: treat R and W as rule-breakers. u+r = /ɜː/; w+a = /ɒ/; w+ar = /ɔː/; w+or = /ɜː/. And the English r has no roll (see /r/).

docs.title: Silent letters
docs.text:
English is full of written letters that are not pronounced. They follow recognisable patterns. Learning the patterns stops Spanish speakers from "spelling-pronouncing" words like doubt, know, should, or hour.

Source: "The phonemes of British English and their spelling" (archived). Organised most-common-first: the top patterns are the ones worth learning today; the rarer ones are further down.

docs.title: Quick map
docs.text: Letter Silent in (main pattern) Flagship examples l -alk, -alm, -alf, -ould, -olk walk, calm, half, would, folk b -mb, -bt climb, thumb, debt, doubt k kn- know, knife, knee w wr-, who-, -wick write, who, Greenwich h wh-, h-, -ah what, hour, honest t -stle, -sten, French -et castle, listen, ballet n -mn autumn, column, hymn g gn-, -gn, -gm gnome, sign, design gh -ight, -ough light, though p ps-, pn-, pt- psychology, pneumonia c -sc- muscle, scissors

docs.title: Silent L — before k, m, f, and in -ould
docs.text:
This is the highest-value one; it is very regular.

  • -alk -> /ɔːk/: walk, talk, chalk, stalk.
  • -alm -> /ɑːm/: calm, palm, balm, psalm, qualm.
  • -alf / -alv -> /ɑːf/, /ɑːv/: half, calf, behalf.
  • -ould: could, should, would.
  • -olk / -olm: folk, yolk, Holmes, Suffolk, Norfolk.
  • also: salmon, almond, Malcolm, Lincoln.

Note: the l is pronounced in many other al words (also, always, salt, bald, false). The silent-l set above is specific; learn it as a list.

docs.title: Silent B — after m (-mb) and before t (-bt)
docs.text:
• -mb -> /m/: climb, comb, crumb, numb, thumb, tomb, womb, lamb, limb, bomb, dumb, plumber.
  • -bt -> /t/: debt, doubt, subtle, subtly.
  • Restored before a vowel suffix: bomb -> bombard.
  • Keeps /b/ (not this pattern): tumble, humble, nimble, assemble.

docs.title: Silent K — initial kn-
docs.text: Always silent before n at the start: know, knowledge, knife, knight, knee, kneel, knock, knot, knit, knob, knuckle.

docs.title: Silent W — wr-, who-, and -wick/-wich names
docs.text:
• wr- -> /r/: write, wrist, wrong, wrap, wreck, wrestle, wring, wriggle.
  • who-words: who, whom, whose, whole, whore.
  • -wich / -wick place names: Greenwich, Norwich, Warwick, Chiswick.
  • also: answer, sword, two.

docs.title: Silent H — initial and wh-
docs.text:
• Silent initial h: hour, honest, honour, heir, vehicle, vehement, annihilate; and words from French.
  • wh- where the w carries the sound (h silent): what, when, where, which, why, while, white, wheel. (These are /w/ in SSBE.)
  • wh- where the h carries the sound (w silent): who, whose, whole.
  • Final h is silent: cheetah, hurrah, oh, pharaoh, shah, verandah.
  • -ham place names: Durham, Nottingham, Chatham, Birmingham.

docs.title: Silent T — -stle, -sten, and French -et/-ot
docs.text:
• -stle -> /sl/: castle, whistle, thistle, bustle, rustle, wrestle, jostle.
  • -sten -> /sn/: listen, fasten, glisten, hasten, moisten, christen.
  • French -et/-ot (final t silent): ballet, beret, buffet, gourmet, cabaret, debut, depot, rapport, ricochet.
  • also: Christmas, mortgage; often (t optional).

docs.title: Silent N — final -mn
docs.text: Silent after m at the end of a word: autumn, column, damn, condemn, hymn, solemn. Restored before a vowel suffix: autumnal, columnist, condemnation, hymnal, solemnity.

docs.title: Silent G — gn- / -gn / -gm
docs.text:
• Initial gn- -> /n/: gnome, gnaw, gnat, gnarl, gnostic.
  • Final -gn -> /n/: sign, design, resign, align, foreign, reign, campaign, champagne, feign, benign, malign, assign, consign.
  • Final -gm -> /m/: diaphragm, paradigm, phlegm.
  • Restored before a vowel suffix: sign -> signal, resign -> resignation, paradigm -> paradigmatic, phlegm -> phlegmatic.

docs.title: GH — silent or /f/
docs.text:
• Silent: light, night, right, sight, high, though, through, bought, daughter, weigh, eight, straight.
  • /f/: enough, rough, tough, cough, laugh, draught.
  • Never a hard /g/+/h/.

docs.title: Silent P — Greek ps-, pn-, pt-
docs.text: psychology, psalm, pseudo, pneumonia, pneumatic, pterodactyl; also corps, coup, receipt, cupboard, raspberry.

docs.title: Silent C — -sc-
docs.text: muscle, scissors, sceptre, scene, science, descend, ascent, corpuscle, fascinate; also indict, victuals (c silent).

docs.title: Silent others
docs.text:
• ch: fuchsia /ˈfjuːʃə/, yacht /jɒt/.
  • s: island, aisle, isle, debris, Illinois.
  • u (after g): guard, guess, guitar, guide, league, tongue, vogue.
  • others: Wednesday (d), handkerchief (d), sandwich (d), colonel (first l).

docs.title: The rule to remember
docs.text: Many silent letters come back when a vowel suffix is added, because the letter then starts a new syllable: autumn -> autumnal, sign -> signal, bomb -> bombard, condemn -> condemnation. If you can hear it in a relative of the word, it is still "there" in the spelling.

docs.title: Common Spanish error
docs.text: The trap: pronouncing every written letter (the b in doubt, the k in know, the l in should, the h in hour, the p in psychology). The fix: learn the top patterns (silent l in walk/calm/would; silent b in climb/debt; silent k in know; silent w in write; silent h in hour). They are regular enough to trust.
