docs.title: Spelling-to-sound rules
docs.text:
English is not phonetic: you cannot always predict pronunciation from spelling. But reliable rules exist. Native children learn them; non-natives are not taught them. They fail sometimes, yet hold in a large share of cases. Always read the mapping both ways: given a letter, which sound; given a sound, which spelling.

This page covers the written syllable rules. The unwritten rules (yod drop, initial E, suffixes, stress shift, hidden sibilants) are in unwritten-rules.md. Per-letter two-angle pages: A, U, OU.

docs.title: The six written syllable rules
docs.text: Rule What happens Examples Closed syllable Vowel is short. bed, dog, went, top, exist, request Open syllable Vowel says its alphabet name. go, he, me, she, admire, stupid Magic e (CVCe) e is silent; vowel says its name. make, rate, like, bake, cube R-controlled Vowel coloured by R. car, short, her, first, turn, learn Vowel team Two vowels; often first is long. brain, meat, please, goal, receive Consonant + le (C+le) Final syllabic l. table, castle, purple

docs.title: Closed syllable
docs.text: A single vowel followed by one or more consonants in the same syllable; the vowel is short: bed, dog, went, top, because, conference, exist, request, event.

docs.title: Open syllable
docs.text: A syllable ending in the vowel; it says its alphabet name: go, he, me, she, information, admire, stupid, exposure.

docs.title: Magic e
docs.text: Consonant + vowel + consonant + e; the e is silent and the vowel says its name: make, rate, like, bake. Full word lists by vowel in reference word lists.

docs.title: R-controlled
docs.text: The R changes the vowel: - ar: car, start, far - or: short, port, cord - ir / ur / ear / er / our: her, first, turn, curve, learn, permanent, journey, nurse, further

docs.title: Vowel team
docs.text:
Two vowels acting together: container, brain, straight, pain, nail, day, lead, meat, sea, reason, please, leave, easy, see, receive, goal, coast, approach, goes, tuesday, venue, due, argue.

Important: a vowel team is almost never read as two Spanish vowels. It spells one sound (a long vowel or a diphthong). See more spelling rules for which teams resemble their spelling (ay/ai/ey, oy/oi, ou/ow), the British /əʊ/ = schwa+ʊ trap, and the highly irregular "ei" team.

docs.title: Consonant + le
docs.text: A final syllabic l: table, castle, purple, little, apple.

docs.title: How to use the rules
docs.text:
1. Split the word into syllables.
  2. Classify each syllable (closed, open, magic-e, R-controlled, vowel team, C+le).
  3. Apply the rule for the vowel.
  4. Watch for R and W, which override the normal rules (see R and W break the vowel rules).
  5. Check against the unwritten rules for suffixes, stress, and the hidden sibilants.

docs.title: Stress and rhythm
docs.text: English is stress-timed; Spanish is syllable-timed. This single difference reshapes the whole rhythm of the language and is why fluent English can sound "swallowed" to a Spanish ear.

docs.title: 1. Stress-timed vs syllable-timed
docs.text:
• Spanish (syllable-timed): every syllable takes roughly the same time. The rhythm is even, like a metronome on each syllable.
  • English (stress-timed): stressed syllables fall at roughly regular intervals, and the unstressed syllables between them are compressed to fit. The rhythm rides on the stressed beats.

Consequence: in English, unstressed syllables shorten and their vowels reduce to schwa. A Spanish speaker giving every syllable full value sounds robotic and is hard to follow.

docs.title: 2. The cues of stress: Spanish vs English
docs.text:
How each language signals that a syllable is stressed:

Cue Spanish English Higher pitch yes yes Louder slightly yes Longer (duration) no (even length) YES (key difference) Vowel quality full vowel in every syllable stressed = full; unstressed = reduced (schwa)

So Spanish marks stress mainly with pitch and a little loudness, while keeping every syllable the same length and its full vowel. English adds a third cue, length, and, crucially, reduces the vowel of unstressed syllables.

Why the schwa is the most common English sound: English has many short, unstressed syllables, and they collapse toward /ə/. The stressed/unstressed contrast is carried largely by vowel quality (full vs schwa), not just pitch. See schwa /ə/.

Learner corollary: do not mark stress the Spanish way (just louder/higher). Make the stressed syllable LONGER, and actively SHORTEN and reduce the others to schwa. Length and reduction are what make it sound English.

Note on pitch: at the phrase level, pitch does a second job, intonation, marking the most important word and signalling meaning, somewhat independently of word stress. See intonation.

docs.title: 3. Word stress
docs.text:
Every multi-syllable word has one main stressed syllable. The stressed syllable is louder, longer, and higher; the rest tend toward schwa.

Getting word stress wrong is often worse than getting a vowel wrong: "PHOtograph / phoTOgraphy / photoGRAPHic" shift stress and change the vowels entirely.

docs.title: Noun vs verb stress shift
docs.text: Many words stress syllable 1 as a noun, syllable 2 as a verb: PROgress / proGRESS, REcord / reCORD, CONtract / conTRACT. See unwritten rules.

docs.title: 4. Sentence stress: content vs function words
docs.text:
At the sentence level the same weakening happens to whole words:

  • Content words (nouns, main verbs, adjectives, adverbs) carry stress.
  • Function words (articles, prepositions, auxiliaries, pronouns, conjunctions) weaken to their weak forms with a schwa.

Example: "I was going to the SHOP to BUY some BREAD." The capitalised content words land on the beat; everything else compresses (was -> /wəz/, to -> /tə/, some -> /səm/).

docs.title: 5. Weak forms
docs.text:
Common function words and their weak (schwa) forms: was /wəz/, been /bɪn/, from /frəm/, of /əv/, and /ən/, to /tə/, for /fə/, can /kən/, them /ðəm/, are /ə/, have /həv/.

See connected speech for how weak forms combine with linking and elision.

docs.title: 6. Common Spanish error
docs.text: The trap: giving every syllable and every word equal weight (syllable-timed rhythm), with full vowels throughout. The fix: find the content words, hit them on the beat, and compress everything between to schwas. Rhythm first, then individual sounds.

docs.title: Word stress
docs.text: Stress is the backbone of English pronunciation. Get the stress right and a word is usually intelligible even with imperfect sounds; get it wrong and correct sounds still fail. Find the stress first, then everything else follows.

docs.title: How to pronounce an unknown word (the procedure)
docs.text:
1. Find the stressed syllable (rules below).
  2. Pronounce the stressed syllable with full value, applying the spelling-to- sound rules (syllable rules, letter pages).
  3. Reduce every unstressed syllable to a schwa (or a short /ɪ/ / /ʊ/ by free variation). Never give an unstressed syllable its full Spanish vowel.
  4. Apply connected-speech changes if the word is in a phrase (connected speech).

This is the single most useful habit: stress first, vowels second, reduction everywhere else.

docs.title: Default: two-syllable words
docs.text:
Most English words are two syllables, and the default depends on word class:

Word class Stress Examples Nouns 1st syllable TAble, WAter, DOCtor, MOUNtain, CARpet Adjectives 1st syllable HAPpy, YELlow, CLEVer, BASic Verbs 2nd syllable deCIDE, reLAX, forGET, aRRIVE, begIN

So the same two syllables lean one way for a noun/adjective and the other for a verb. This is a tendency, not a law; there are many exceptions (e.g. the verb "VIsit", "PROmise" stress the first; the noun "hoTEL", "maCHINE" stress the second).

docs.title: Noun/adjective vs verb: same spelling, different stress
docs.text:
A set of words shift stress by class: the noun/adjective stresses syllable 1, the verb stresses syllable 2. Vowels reduce accordingly. This is a summary; the full four-class treatment (standard shifters, always-first, always-second, and sound-change pairs like use/use and house/house) is in noun/verb pairs.

Word Noun/adj Verb record REcord reCORD progress PROgress proGRESS present PREsent preSENT contract CONtract conTRACT project PROject proJECT rebel REbel reBEL export EXport exPORT permit PERmit perMIT conduct CONduct conDUCT object OBject obJECT increase INcrease inCREASE

Caveats: - Not all same-spelled pairs shift: "comment", "promise", "focus", "profit" keep first-syllable stress for both noun and verb. - Some can be stressed either way without changing meaning much (regional or free variation): "address", "research", "detail" (noun) vary by accent (UK often REsearch vs US reSEARCH). - Learn the common shifting set; do not assume every pair shifts.

docs.title: Suffix-driven stress
docs.text:
Many suffixes fix the stress position. The most reliable:

Suffix Stress falls on Examples -tion, -sion syllable before the suffix eduCAtion, deCIsion, naTIONal (penult) -ic syllable before -ic eCOnomic, fanTAStic, phoTOgraphic -ity syllable before -ity aBIlity, possiBIlity, actiVIty -ial, -ian syllable before it esSENtial, muSIcian -ious, -eous syllable before it inDUStrious, outRAgeous -ify third from end iDENtify, CLAssify

Rule of thumb for -tion/-sion/-ic/-ity/-ial: stress the syllable immediately before the suffix (the penultimate syllable of the whole word).

docs.title: Suffixes usually change vowel quality, NOT stress
docs.text:
Most derivational suffixes are unstressed: they often change the suffix vowel (schwa <-> full) while the stress stays on the root. The clearest case is -ate verbs:

  • -ate: noun/adjective /ət/ vs verb /eɪt/, but the stress does not move. DElegate (n /ət/) -> DElegate (v /eɪt/); ESTimate, SEParate, MODerate, ADvocate, DUPlicate, APProximate, GRADuate, ALTernate, arTICulate, deLIBerate, eLABorate, asSOCiate. Only the suffix vowel changes; the stressed syllable is unchanged.
  • -ine (unstressed /ɪn/, not /aɪn/): deTERmine, eXAMine, iMAGine, GENuine, MEDicine, DIScipline, FAMine, enGINE. Stress on the root, suffix reduced.
  • Other usually-unstressed endings: -age (VILLage, MANage, PACKage), -ace (PALace, SURface, MENace), -ous (FAMous, DANGerous), -ure (NATure, CULture), -ive (NEGative, OBjective keeps root stress).

Takeaway: when a word has one of these endings, find the stress on the ROOT, then reduce the suffix. The suffix is a passenger, not the driver.

Self-stressed suffixes (the exceptions: these DO take the stress themselves): -ee (emploYEE, trainEE, refuGEE, guaranTEE), -eer (engiNEER, volunTEER, pioNEER), -ese (japaNESE, portuGUESE, chiNESE), -ette (cigaRETTE, kitcheNETTE), -esque (pictuRESQUE, groTESQUE), -oon (balLOON, carTOON), -aire (millionAIRE), -ade (lemonADE).

Stress-neutral suffixes (do not move the stress of the base): -ly, -ness, -ment, -ful, -less, -er, -ing, -ed. So HAPpy -> HAPpily, GOVern -> GOVernment.

docs.title: R-controlled syllables attract stress
docs.text:
An r-coloured syllable (vowel + r giving /ɜː/, /ɑː/, /ɔː/) is heavy and tends to pull the stress onto itself. Useful as a tie-breaker when you are unsure which syllable is stressed: the r-syllable is a strong candidate. Works across word classes and word lengths, not just two-syllable verbs.

  • Verbs (2-syl): preFER, reCUR, conCERN, deTER, aLERT, deSERVE, obSERVE, reTURN, disTURB, preSERVE, conVERT, eMERGE, inCUR, aVERT.
  • Verbs (3+ syl): deTERmine, disCERN, reaFFIRM, misinTERpret (on -ter-), reHEARSE, reiMBURSE.
  • Nouns (2-syl): conCERN, reTURN, deSSERT (/z/), reWARD, suPPORT.
  • Nouns (3+ syl): perFORMance, imPORtance, dePARture, disORder, obSERver, conVERsion, deTERminant.
  • Adjectives: abSURD, aLERT, perVERSE, suPERB, eTERnal, inFORmal, exTERnal (on -ter-), noCTURNal (on -tur-), deTERminate.
  • Longer words where the r-syllable carries primary stress: perFORMance, conSERvative (on -ser-), obSERvatory (on -ser-), alTERNative (on -ter-), comFORTable (on -for-), deTERmination (secondary on -ter-, primary -na-).

This is a tendency, not a law. Counter-cases where the stress is elsewhere: WAter, MANner, CORner, MURmur, GOVernor (first syllable). And suffix-driven words still obey their suffix rule (uniVERsity stresses -ver- by the -ity rule, which here happens to be the r-syllable too).

docs.title: Stress shift under suffixation
docs.text:
Adding a suffix can move the stress and change every vowel:

PHOtograph -> phoTOgraphy -> photoGRAPHic. POLitics -> poLItical -> politiCIAN PERson -> perSONify

This is why the same root sounds so different across its family: the stress moves, and the vowels reduce around the new stressed syllable.

docs.title: Primary and secondary stress
docs.text:
Long words (often those with suffixes) have two stresses: - Primary stress: the strongest syllable (marked ˈ in IPA). - Secondary stress: a weaker beat earlier in the word (marked ˌ), often where the base word used to be stressed.

Examples: ˌpronunciˈation, ˌuniverˈsity (no), ˌeduˈcation, ˌpossiˈbility, ˌinterˈnational. The secondary stress keeps long words rhythmic; the syllables between the two stresses reduce to schwa.

docs.title: Common Spanish error
docs.text: The trap: flat, even stress (Spanish is syllable-timed), or stressing the wrong syllable, which can make a word unrecognisable. The fix: learn the stress first. Two-syllable nouns/adjectives -> 1st; verbs -> 2nd; -tion/-ic/-ity -> penult. Then reduce everything unstressed to schwa.

docs.title: British vs American differences
docs.text: Reference accent is SSBE. There are 8 main pronunciation differences to American: 5 vowels, 3 consonants. Plus grammar and vocabulary differences.

docs.title: Vowel differences (5)
docs.text:
1. Short O. British pronounces an O; American pronounces a back /ɑ/ (a back a, like long a but not long). Exception: when followed by R. Biggest vowel difference. hot, lost, dock, stock.
  2. Long /ɑː/ distribution. Not a different sound, but British uses it in many more words. Beyond the +R cases (long a in both), British says past, path, class, last with long /ɑː/; American uses /æ/.
  3. /əʊ/ vs /oʊ/ (the "home" diphthong). American pronounces it like the Spanish "casa" o; British replaces the o with a schwa (/əʊ/). Very characteristic. home, go, so, road.
  4. Centring diphthongs from final R. Words ending in R: British does not pronounce the final R and substitutes a schwa. Very noticeable. fair, here, tour → /eə/, /ɪə/, /ʊə/.
  5. Front /æ/. American makes it a kind of "ea" diphthong (and nasalizes it more, especially in the South). cat.

docs.title: Consonant differences (3)
docs.text:
1. Yod drop (/j/ drop). American dropped the yod in many words that keep it in British. during, dual, tune → British /dj-/ (→ /dʒ/ by assimilation), American /d-/. Some common American words still keep it.
  2. Rhoticity. American is generally rhotic; British is non-rhotic. Consequence: in the long schwa /ɜː/, British holds a long sound; American must fit the R in, so the schwa is shorter.
  3. T. American uses the flap t in unstressed syllables (like a Spanish R): better, city. British uses a normal T, though some British accents use a glottal t far more.

docs.title: Flap T detail
docs.text:
• American: flap t inside the word (better, city).
  • British: flap t mainly when linking words (as in "But I"); increasingly common but primarily at word boundaries.

docs.title: Elasticity
docs.text: British is more elastic: the long/short vowel distinction is more evident. IPA transcriptions often show the two dots (ː) for British and drop them for American.

docs.title: Unwritten rules
docs.text: The reliable patterns that native children absorb but that are never written in a grammar for learners. They fail sometimes but hold in a great many cases. For the written syllable rules (closed, open, magic-e, R-controlled, vowel team, C+le) see spelling-to-sound rules.

docs.title: Rule 1 — yod drop after L or R
docs.text: Open-syllable U is /juː/, but the yod drops after L or R, even in British: conclusion, include (L), rude, blue (R). Americans drop it far more widely (tune, duke, student, news). Full treatment in the letter U.

docs.title: Rule 2 — initial unstressed E = short /ɪ/
docs.text:
Word starts consonant + E, and the 2nd syllable is stressed: that E becomes a short /ɪ/, almost always.

regarding, reverse, description, result, deserve, redundancy, enable, defect, effect, default, evolve, severe, device, security, delivery, evaluation, event, credential, present, report, decision, encrypt.

docs.title: Rule 3 — -AW / -AU = /ɔː/
docs.text:
Always an O sound, never the Spanish "au". American often turns it into a back /ɑ/.

default, caught, taught, faulty, launch, cause, because, clause, pause, australia, author, audience, august, autumn, audit, authorization, audio.

docs.title: Rule 4 — suffix -ate: noun/adjective vs verb
docs.text: Part of speech Sound Examples noun / adjective /ət/ candidate, certificate, climate, appropriate, delegate (n) verb /eɪt/ integrate, fluctuate, separate (v), delegate (v)

docs.title: Rule 5 — noun/adjective vs verb stress shift
docs.text:
Same spelling; the standard shifters stress syllable 1 as a noun/adjective and syllable 2 as a verb, with the vowels reducing accordingly:

PROgress / proGRESS, REcord / reCORD, PREsent / preSENT, CONtract / conTRACT, PROject / proJECT, EXport / exPORT, REbel / reBEL, PERmit / perMIT.

Caution: not every same-spelled pair shifts. "comment", "request", "command" do not. And some pairs change a SOUND rather than the stress (use /juːs/ vs /juːz/, house, close). Full four-class treatment in noun/verb pairs.

docs.title: Rule 6 — which spellings hide /ʃ/, /ʒ/, /z/
docs.text:
• /ʃ/: not only sh, also -tion, -ssion, -cious, -cial, -cian, s+u (sure).
  • /ʒ/: -sion after a vowel (vision), -sure (measure), genre.
  • /z/: s between vowels (easy), is/was/as/his, -ize/-ise, ex- (exam, example).

See /ʃ/, /ʒ/, /z/.

docs.title: Rule 7 — free variation of the schwa
docs.text: In some unstressed syllables the schwa can be replaced by short /ɪ/ or /ʊ/ (mostly /ɪ/). The distance is tiny; it does not matter. Never use a full Spanish vowel. See schwa.

docs.title: Rule 8 — unstable vowel teams OU / UI / EA
docs.text: No fixed rule; each word is learned. OU has ~11 values (see the letters OU); EA varies (beat /iː/, head /e/, great /eɪ/, heart /ɑː/).

docs.title: Vowel: /æ/ (front a)
docs.text: Not a major problem for Spanish speakers: the Spanish "a" is already fairly front, so /æ/ (cat) is close enough. The hard one is the long back /ɑː/. Still worth separating /æ/ from /ʌ/ and /e/.

docs.title: 1. What it is
docs.text:
/æ/ is a short, open, front vowel, between Spanish "a" and "e". It is the vowel in "cat", "bad", "trap". In SSBE it is a flat, fairly open sound; in American it is often more diphthong-like (/eə/) and more nasal.

Spanish contrast: Spanish has no exact /æ/, but the Spanish "a" is fairly front, so /æ/ is one of the easier non-Spanish vowels. The minor risk is drifting toward /ɒ/ (cat -> cot) or merging with /ʌ/ and /e/. The genuinely hard back vowel is /ɑː/.

docs.title: 2. How to produce it
docs.text: Open the mouth as for Spanish "a", then move the tongue forward and slightly up toward "e", and spread the lips a little. Short. It should feel like an "a" leaning toward "e".

docs.title: 3. Angle 1 — when a spelling makes /æ/
docs.text:
Almost always a written "a" in a closed, stressed syllable.

Spelling Examples a (closed syllable) cat, bad, trap, hat, man, map, back, apple, random a (closed, multi-syllable) contract, impact, diagram, artifact, abstract

docs.title: 4. Angle 2 — where the /æ/ sound is written
docs.text:
/æ/ is essentially always a written "a" in a closed syllable:

cat, bad, trap, hat, man, map, cash, back, apple, random, contract, impact, diagram, transition, artifact, blackboard, abstract.

TRAP-BATH caveat (UK): some closed-"a" words take long /ɑː/ in SSBE instead (past, path, class, last, dance). In American those stay /æ/. See the letter A.

docs.title: 5. Minimal pairs / contrasts
docs.text: Pair Contrast hat / hot /æ/ vs /ɒ/ cat / cut /æ/ vs /ʌ/ bad / bed /æ/ vs /e/ ran / run /æ/ vs /ʌ/ cap / cup /æ/ vs /ʌ/ bat / bet /æ/ vs /e/

docs.title: 6. Common Spanish error
docs.text: The trap: using the back Spanish "a", so cat sounds like "cot". The fix: push the tongue forward toward "e" and spread the lips. Contrast with /ʌ/ (cat/cut) and /ɒ/ (hat/hot) to place it correctly.

docs.title: Vowel: /ɔː/ (the "aw" o)
docs.text: A long, rounded, mid-back vowel. The -aw/-au spellings always give this sound, never the Spanish "au".

docs.title: 1. What it is
docs.text:
/ɔː/ is a long, rounded, mid-back vowel, the sound in "thought", "law", "caught", "north". Longer and more rounded than /ɒ/.

Spanish contrast: Spanish has no long rounded vowel like this. Spanish speakers read "au" as a Spanish diphthong (a + u), which is wrong.

docs.title: 2. How to produce it
docs.text: Tongue mid-back, lips rounded, held long. More rounded and higher than /ɒ/.

docs.title: 3. Angle 1 — when a spelling makes /ɔː/
docs.text: Spelling Examples aw law, saw, draw, dawn, awful au cause, author, launch, autumn, August, audio or short, port, cord, north, sort, born ou (+ght/r) thought, bought, brought, ought, course, four, source oor / oar / ar(w) door, floor, board, war, warm al (some) all, call, tall, walk, talk, salt, false

docs.title: 4. Angle 2 — where the /ɔː/ sound is written
docs.text: aw: law, saw, draw, dawn, awful, lawn. au: default, caught, taught, faulty, launch, cause, because, clause, pause, australia, author, audience, august, autumn, audit, authorization, audio. or: short, port, cord, north, sort, born, horse, morning. ough/ought: thought, bought, brought, ought, nought. our/oor/oar: course, court, four, source, your, board, door, floor. al: all, call, tall, walk, talk, salt, false, bald. war-: war, warm, ward, dwarf.

docs.title: 5. Minimal pairs / contrasts

docs.title: 6. Common Spanish error
docs.text: The trap: reading au/aw as the Spanish diphthong "au" (a-u), so "cause" becomes "ca-use". The fix: one long rounded O sound. au = aw = /ɔː/. Note: American often turns this into a back /ɑ/ in many au words.

docs.title: Vowel: /e/ (short e)
docs.text: A short, front mid vowel. Close to Spanish "e", so relatively easy; the work is the contrasts with /æ/ and /ɪ/.

docs.title: 1. What it is
docs.text:
/e/ (also written /ɛ/) is a short, front, mid vowel, the sound in "bed", "red", "head". Close to the Spanish "e".

Spanish contrast: very close to Spanish /e/, so one of the easiest. The risk is confusing it with /æ/ (bed/bad) and, in weak syllables, with /ɪ/.

docs.title: 2. How to produce it
docs.text: Tongue front and mid, lips slightly spread, short. Essentially the Spanish "e", kept short.

docs.title: 3. Angle 1 — when a spelling makes /e/
docs.text: Spelling Examples e (closed syllable) bed, red, pen, ten, when, left, send ea head, bread, dead, health, weather, ready a (rare) many, any, said, again ai (rare) said, again

docs.title: 4. Angle 2 — where the /e/ sound is written
docs.text: e (closed): bed, red, pen, ten, when, left, send, best, help, egg. ea: head, bread, dead, health, weather, ready, breakfast, measure (stem). a: many, any. ai: said, again, against. ie (rare): friend. eo (rare): leopard, jeopardy.

docs.title: 6. Common Spanish error
docs.text: The trap: merging /e/ with /æ/, so bed = bad. The fix: /e/ is the Spanish "e"; /æ/ is more open and leans toward "a". Train bed/bad and pen/pin to lock the boundaries.

docs.title: Vowel: long a /ɑː/ (back a)
docs.text: One of the top-four priority vowels for Spanish speakers, and the hard "a". A long, open, back vowel. In SSBE it reaches many more words than in American (the TRAP-BATH split). The front /æ/ is easy by comparison; this is the foreign one.

docs.title: 1. What it is
docs.text:
/ɑː/ is a long, open, back vowel, the sound in "car", "father", "past" (UK). Open like Spanish "a" but further back and held long.

Spanish contrast: Spanish "a" is central and short. Spanish speakers make it too short and too front, and often add a rolled R in "car".

docs.title: 2. How to produce it
docs.text: Open the mouth wide, tongue low and back, lips neutral, held long. In British English (non-rhotic), do not pronounce a following R; the long vowel carries the sound.

docs.title: 3. Angle 1 — when a spelling makes /ɑː/
docs.text: Spelling Examples a + R car, start, far, hard, park, large, March a (UK TRAP-BATH) past, path, class, last, fast, bath, dance, chance al (silent l) calm, palm, half, calf a (foreign / misc) father, drama, tomato (UK)

docs.title: 4. Angle 2 — where the /ɑː/ sound is written
docs.text: a + R: car, start, far, hard, park, large, March, garden, sharp. a (UK only, TRAP-BATH): past, path, class, last, fast, bath, dance, chance, grass, ask, after, example, command. al (silent l): calm, palm, half, calf. foreign: father, drama, banana (final), tomato (UK).

docs.title: 5. Minimal pairs / contrasts

docs.title: 6. Common Spanish error
docs.text: The trap: a short, front Spanish "a" plus a rolled R in "car". The fix: open, back, and long; no R in British English. For TRAP-BATH words, remember SSBE uses /ɑː/ where American uses /æ/.

docs.title: Vowel: long i /iː/
docs.text: The tense, long counterpart of /ɪ/. Spanish speakers produce it fairly well, but must keep it distinct from /ɪ/.

docs.title: 1. What it is
docs.text:
/iː/ is a long, tense, high front vowel, close to the Spanish "i" but longer and tenser. It is the vowel in "sheep", "beat", "see".

Spanish contrast: close to Spanish /i/, so it is one of the easier sounds. The real work is keeping it separate from the short lax /ɪ/.

docs.title: 2. How to produce it
docs.text: Tongue high and front, lips spread as if smiling, held long and tense. More tension and length than Spanish "i".

docs.title: 3. Angle 1 — when a spelling makes /iː/
docs.text: Spelling Examples ee see, sheep, feet, green, tree ea beat, sea, please, reason, leave, easy e (open syllable) he, me, she, these, complete ie field, believe, piece ei (after c) receive, ceiling, deceive i (some loanwords) machine, police, ski, pizza y (final) happy, city, funny (weak, between /i/ and /ɪ/)

docs.title: 4. Angle 2 — where the /iː/ sound is written
docs.text: ee: see, sheep, feet, green, tree, agree. ea: beat, sea, please, reason, leave, easy, meat, team. e / e-e: he, me, she, these, complete, eve. ie: field, believe, piece, chief. ei: receive, ceiling, deceive, seize. i: machine, police, ski, litre, pizza, visa.

docs.title: 5. Minimal pairs / contrasts
docs.text: See the full /ɪ/ vs /iː/ table on short i /ɪ/: ship/sheep, bit/beat, live/leave, sit/seat, fit/feet, rich/reach, it/eat.

docs.title: 6. Common Spanish error
docs.text: The trap: collapsing /iː/ and /ɪ/ into one Spanish "i", so sheep = ship. The fix: /iː/ is long and tense (smile); /ɪ/ is short and lax (relaxed). Always train as a pair.

docs.title: Vowel: long schwa /ɜː/
docs.text: The second most important vowel for Spanish speakers. A long, stressed central vowel that almost no Spanish native produces correctly.

docs.title: 1. What it is
docs.text:
/ɜː/ is a long, central vowel that always carries stress. Think of it as a stressed, lengthened cousin of the schwa, held longer and said with intent. It is the vowel in "bird", "her", "turn".

Spanish contrast: it does not exist in Spanish. Spanish speakers substitute a full vowel (usually /e/ or /a/) plus a rolled R, which sounds foreign and often breaks the word.

Note on accent: in SSBE (non-rhotic) the R after it is silent and the vowel is held long. In American (rhotic) the R is pronounced, so the vowel is shorter and R-coloured (often written /ɝ/).

docs.title: 2. How to produce it
docs.text: Tongue central and mid, like the schwa, but hold it and give it full voice and length. Lips neutral, slightly spread. In British English, do not pronounce the R that follows; let the vowel carry the whole sound.

docs.title: 3. Angle 1 — when a spelling makes /ɜː/
docs.text:
The sound is almost always a vowel + R in a stressed syllable.

Spelling Examples ir bird, girl, first, shirt, birth, circle, virgin, confirm ur turn, purge, curve, further, turtle, burst, disturb er her, term, server, concern, observe, reverse, emerge, personal ear learn, earth, heard, search, early wor world, work, worse, worth, worm (w + or is the exception that gives /ɜː/, not /ɔː/)

docs.title: 4. Angle 2 — where the /ɜː/ sound is written
docs.text: Spelling Examples Notes ur purpose, purge, precursor, disturb, burglary, burst, turbulence, further, turn wor world, work, worse, worth, worm, worry (US) NOT "worn" (/ɔː/) er permanent, jersey, server, permit, emerge, versus, observe, reverse, concern, personal NOT "merely" ir confirm, bird, girl, virgin, circle, shirt, birth ear learn, earth, heard, early, search

docs.title: 6. Common Spanish error
docs.text: The trap: saying a full Spanish vowel plus a rolled R (e.g. "bird" as "berd" with a tapped r). The fix: one long central vowel, no R movement in British English. The tongue barely moves; the sound is held, not rolled.

docs.title: Vowel: long u /uː/
docs.text: A long, tense, rounded, high-back vowel. Often preceded by a yod /j/, which Americans (and British after L/R) drop.

docs.title: 1. What it is
docs.text:
/uː/ is a long, tense, rounded high-back vowel, the sound in "food", "blue", "tune". Often appears as /juː/ (with a yod) in spelling with u.

Spanish contrast: close to a long Spanish "u", so the vowel itself is easy. The work is the yod (/juː/ vs /uː/) and keeping it distinct from short /ʊ/.

docs.title: 2. How to produce it
docs.text: Tongue high and back, firm lip rounding, held long and tense. For /juː/, start with a short y-glide (/j/) then the vowel.

docs.title: 3. Angle 1 — when a spelling makes /uː/ (or /juː/)
docs.text: Spelling Sound Examples u (open / magic e) /juː/ (UK), /uː/ (US) cube, cute, tune, duke, use, music u after L/R /uː/ (yod drops) rude, blue, June, conclusion, include oo /uː/ food, moon, soon, pool, cool ou /uː/ group, soup, route, through, youth ew /juː/ or /uː/ few, new, flew, chew ue /uː/ or /juː/ blue, true, due, argue

docs.title: 4. Angle 2 — where the /uː/ sound is written
docs.text:
oo: food, moon, soon, pool, cool, room, boot, zoo. ou: group, soup, route, through, youth, wound. u / u-e: rude, June, flute, include, conclusion, super. ew: few, new, flew, chew, crew. ue: blue, true, due, argue, clue. o (rare): do, who, move, prove, lose, tomb.

Yod-drop list (/juː/ -> /uː/ in US, and after L/R in UK): tune, duke, due, during, reduce, produce, stupid, student, news, Tuesday, resume, consume, suit, enthusiasm. Full list in the letter U.

Yod rule (from the source): /j/ before /uː/ appears with spellings u, ue, eu, ew, ure unless preceded by j, ch, r, or consonant+l. So "new, few, cue" keep the yod; "Jew, chew, crew, blue, prune" drop it.

docs.title: 5. Minimal pairs / contrasts
docs.text: Pair Contrast fool / full /uː/ vs /ʊ/ pool / pull /uː/ vs /ʊ/ Luke / look /uː/ vs /ʊ/ food / foot /uː/ vs /ʊ/

docs.title: 6. Common Spanish error
docs.text: The trap: ignoring the yod, so "music" loses its /j/; or confusing /uː/ with short /ʊ/ (fool/full). The fix: keep /uː/ long and tense; add the yod for u in open syllables (cube = /kjuːb/), but drop it after L and R (rude, blue).

docs.title: Vowel: schwa /ə/
docs.text: Standard sound-page template. The most important sound in English for a Spanish speaker. Master this before anything else.

docs.title: 1. What it is
docs.text:
/ə/ is the "schwa": a short, relaxed, neutral vowel. It is the most frequent vowel in English and appears only in unstressed syllables. It never carries stress.

Spanish contrast: Spanish has no schwa. Spanish gives every written vowel its full value, in every syllable. This is the single biggest pronunciation error Spanish speakers make. Spanish speakers also never delete a weak vowel, which English does.

docs.title: 2. How to produce it
docs.text:
Relax the tongue to the centre of the mouth, neither high nor low, neither front nor back. Lips neutral. Make the shortest, laziest voiced vowel you can. It is the sound of effort reduced to almost nothing: the "a" in "about", the "er" in "mother".

Key idea: the schwa is produced by doing less, not more. If you are moving your mouth deliberately, it is wrong.

docs.title: 3. Angle 1 — when a written vowel becomes /ə/
docs.text:
Any written vowel reduces to schwa when its syllable is unstressed.

Spelling Example Reduced syllable a banana, about, alarm ba-NA-na e problem, taken PROB-lem o common, method COM-mon u support, album sup-PORT i pencil, family PEN-cil ar/er/or/ur mother, doctor, sugar MOTH-er

Rule of thumb: find the stressed syllable; most of the rest tend to schwa.

docs.title: 4. Angle 2 — where the /ə/ sound appears
docs.text:
Seen (predictable): international, document, thorough, america, alarm, alert, academy, banana, parameter, corporate, product, mayor, neutral, finally, fur, further, backward, compatible, mandatory, capacity.

Not obvious: proprietary, precious, supply, ireland, natural, model, devil, perimeter, composure, amateur, favorite, conclusion, interest, informative, opinion, average, pronunciation, image, raise, functionality, dictionary, responsible, affirmation, level, ocean, install, installation.

docs.title: Schwa deletion (syncope)
docs.text:
The schwa often disappears entirely before L, N, R (sometimes M, T):

Dropped before Examples R temperature, literature, literally, chocolate, every, general, different, history, separate, camera, salary, reference, average, delivery N personal, prisoner, pleasant, thousand, chosen, risen L family, basically, automatically, especially, table, phrasal, omelet

docs.title: 5. Minimal pairs / contrasts
docs.text:
The schwa itself rarely forms minimal pairs; its importance is rhythmic. The contrast that matters is schwa vs a full Spanish vowel:

  • "banana" with three schwas (bə-NA-nə) vs the Spanish "ba-na-na".
  • "the" weak /ðə/ vs a stressed /ðiː/.

docs.title: Free variation
docs.text: In some unstressed syllables the schwa can be replaced by a short /ɪ/ or /ʊ/, mostly /ɪ/. The phonetic distance is tiny, so it does not matter. What matters: never substitute a full Spanish vowel.

docs.title: 6. Common Spanish error
docs.text: The trap: pronouncing every syllable with its full written vowel. The fix: identify the stress, then weaken everything else to a schwa. A schwa in the wrong place is far better than a full Spanish vowel.

docs.title: 7. Practice
docs.text: See study links: "Schwa", "Schwa drop", and "Schwa never stressed".

docs.title: Vowel: /ʌ/ (the "hat" a)
docs.text: The short, central "cut" vowel. Spanish speakers tend to read it as the written letter instead of this sound.

docs.title: 1. What it is
docs.text:
/ʌ/ is a short, central-open vowel, the sound in "cut", "love", "much". In the IPA notes here it is informally the "a with a hat" symbol.

Spanish contrast: no direct equivalent. Because it is spelled with u, o, or ou, Spanish speakers read the letter (u as /u/, o as /o/) instead of producing /ʌ/.

docs.title: 2. How to produce it
docs.text: Central, relaxed, slightly open. Close to a stressed schwa but a touch more open. Short. Lips neutral, not rounded (rounding is the main error with "o" and "u" spellings).

docs.title: 3. Angle 1 — when a spelling makes /ʌ/
docs.text: Spelling Examples u (closed syllable) cut, much, sun, but, run, under, sudden, judge, luxury o love, come, some, money, mother, month, front, among ou enough, young, couple, touch, rough, country, encourage oo (rare) blood, flood

docs.title: 4. Angle 2 — where the /ʌ/ sound is written
docs.text: u (closed): culture, public, much, cut, redundancy, concurrent, under, ugly, fun, sunday, drunk, judge, pulse, sudden, assumption, luxury, summary, sublimate, bubble, up. o: love, come, some, money, mother, month, front, among, nothing, oven. ou: enough, young, couple, touch, rough, country, encourage. oo: blood, flood.

docs.title: 5. Minimal pairs / contrasts
docs.text: Pair Contrast cut / cat /ʌ/ vs /æ/ cup / cap /ʌ/ vs /æ/ run / ran /ʌ/ vs /æ/ luck / lock /ʌ/ vs /ɒ/ come / calm /ʌ/ vs /ɑː/ cut / could /ʌ/ vs /ʊ/

docs.title: 6. Common Spanish error
docs.text: The trap: reading the letter, so "cut" becomes "coot" (/u/) and "love" becomes "lov" (/o/). The fix: ignore the spelling; produce a short central unrounded vowel. No lip rounding. Contrast cut/cat and luck/lock to place it.

docs.title: Vowel: short i /ɪ/
docs.text: One of the top-four vowels for Spanish speakers. The problem is quality, not length. Very common, and many minimal pairs with /iː/.

docs.title: 1. What it is
docs.text:
/ɪ/ is a short, lax, relaxed vowel, higher and more relaxed than Spanish "i". It is the vowel in "ship", "bit", "live". It is extremely common in English.

Spanish contrast: Spanish has only one "i" sound, the tense /i/. Spanish speakers replace /ɪ/ with that tense /i/, so "ship" sounds like "sheep". The error is quality (tense vs lax), not just length.

docs.title: 2. How to produce it
docs.text: Start from the Spanish "i", then relax the tongue slightly down and back, and loosen the lips. Shorter and looser than /iː/. Do not smile or spread the lips; that produces the tense /iː/.

docs.title: 3. Angle 1 — when a spelling makes /ɪ/
docs.text: Spelling Examples i (closed syllable) ship, bit, live, sit, big, fish, lip y (closed / medial) gym, system, myth, crystal e (initial unstressed) regarding, result, decision, event (see unwritten rules) -ed /ɪd/ ending wanted, needed, started -age, -ate (reduced) village, image, climate, private

docs.title: 4. Angle 2 — where the /ɪ/ sound is written
docs.text: Spelling Examples i ship, bit, live, sit, big, fish, will, mix y gym, system, myth, crystal, symbol e (weak / initial) enough, before, decide, remember, pretty ui build, guild a (some -age/-ate) village, cottage, climate, private, senate ee (rare weak) coffee, committee (final, between /ɪ/ and /i/)

docs.title: 5. Minimal pairs / contrasts
docs.text:
The /ɪ/ vs /iː/ contrast is one of the most important for Spanish speakers.

/ɪ/ /iː/ ship sheep bit beat live leave sit seat fit feet rich reach it eat fill feel

docs.title: 6. Common Spanish error
docs.text: The trap: using the tense Spanish /i/ for every written "i", so ship -> sheep. The fix: relax. /ɪ/ is loose and short; /iː/ is tense and long. Train them as pairs (ship/sheep) until the quality difference is automatic.

docs.title: Vowel: short o /ɒ/
docs.text: A short, rounded, open-back vowel. This is the clearest UK/US vowel difference: American replaces it with a back /ɑ/.

docs.title: 1. What it is
docs.text:
/ɒ/ is a short, rounded, open back vowel, the sound in "hot", "lost", "dock" in SSBE. It exists in British English but not in General American.

Spanish contrast: Spanish "o" is more closed and not this open. Spanish speakers use a tenser "o". American speakers use an unrounded back /ɑ/.

docs.title: 2. How to produce it
docs.text: Open the mouth, tongue low and back, with light lip rounding. Short. Less rounded and more open than Spanish "o".

docs.title: 3. Angle 1 — when a spelling makes /ɒ/
docs.text: Spelling Examples o (closed syllable) hot, lost, dock, stock, top, box, god, clock a (after w/qu) want, wash, watch, quality, squad ou (rare) cough, trough

docs.title: 4. Angle 2 — where the /ɒ/ sound is written
docs.text: o (closed): hot, lost, dock, stock, top, box, god, clock, shop, rock, odd. a (after w, qu): want, wash, watch, what, quality, squad, quantity. ou: cough, trough. au (some, UK): because (variant), sausage.

docs.title: 5. Minimal pairs / contrasts
docs.text: Pair Contrast hot / hat /ɒ/ vs /æ/ lock / luck /ɒ/ vs /ʌ/ cot / caught /ɒ/ vs /ɔː/ pot / port /ɒ/ vs /ɔː/ not / nought /ɒ/ vs /ɔː/

docs.title: 6. Common Spanish error
docs.text: The trap: a closed, tense Spanish "o". The fix: open the mouth more and round the lips only lightly. Keep it short. Note: in American this sound becomes an unrounded back /ɑ/ (hot = "haht").

docs.title: Vowel: short u /ʊ/
docs.text: A short, lax, rounded, high-back vowel. The closed-syllable exceptions (put, push, bull) and the /uː/ contrast are the traps.

docs.title: 1. What it is
docs.text:
/ʊ/ is a short, lax, rounded high-back vowel, the sound in "put", "book", "could". The short, relaxed counterpart of /uː/.

Spanish contrast: Spanish "u" is tense. Spanish speakers use that tense /u/ and fail to distinguish /ʊ/ from /uː/ (full/fool).

docs.title: 2. How to produce it
docs.text: Tongue high and back, light lip rounding, relaxed and short. Looser and shorter than /uː/.

docs.title: 3. Angle 1 — when a spelling makes /ʊ/
docs.text: Spelling Examples u (closed exceptions) put, push, bull, pull, full, bullet oo book, good, foot, look, wood, cook ou could, should, would o (rare) woman, wolf

docs.title: 4. Angle 2 — where the /ʊ/ sound is written
docs.text: u (exceptions to the /ʌ/ rule): put, push, bull, pull, full, bullet. oo: book, good, foot, look, wood, cook, stood, hook. ou: could, should, would. o: woman, wolf. Weak -ure endings (variant): exposure, measure, culture (schwa or /ʊ/).

docs.title: 5. Minimal pairs / contrasts
docs.text: Pair Contrast full / fool /ʊ/ vs /uː/ pull / pool /ʊ/ vs /uː/ look / Luke /ʊ/ vs /uː/ could / cooed /ʊ/ vs /uː/ put / putt /ʊ/ vs /ʌ/

docs.title: 6. Common Spanish error
docs.text: The trap: using tense Spanish /u/ for both /ʊ/ and /uː/, so full = fool. The fix: /ʊ/ is short and lax; /uː/ is long and tense. Remember the closed-syllable exceptions (put, push, bull, pull) that take /ʊ/, not /ʌ/.
